title: PFH-loaded hollow iron oxide nanoparticles suppress breast cancer progression through magnetothermal ferroptosis and inhibition of TGF-β1/Smad-driven EMT.
abstract: Breast cancer metastasis remains a major cause of mortality, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a key process driving tumor progression. Here, we developed perfluorohexane-loaded hollow iron oxide nanoparticles (PFH-HIONs) as a magnetothermal phase-transition platform for image-guided breast cancer therapy. PFH-HIONs were synthesized by vacuum-assisted loading of PFH into hollow iron oxide nanoparticles and characterized for morphology, size, zeta potential, magnetothermal performance, and ultrasound phase-transition behavior. Their antitumor effects were evaluated in MCF-7 cells and in a xenograft model. Ferroptosis-related changes, EMT-associated signaling, macrophage polarization, and immune-related responses were further assessed. PFH-HIONs showed a hollow nanostructure, AMF-responsive heating, and stimulus-triggered ultrasound contrast enhancement. PFH-HIONs combined with AMF reduced MCF-7 cell viability and increased apoptotic cell death. This treatment also induced ferroptosis-related changes, including GPX4 downregulation, 4-HNE and ACSL4 upregulation, and ROS accumulation. In TGF-β1-treated MCF-7 cells, PFH-HION plus AMF suppressed Smad2/3 phosphorylation, reversed EMT-associated protein and transcription factor expression, and these effects were partially attenuated by ferrostatin-1. In addition, PFH-HIONs plus AMF promoted a more pro-inflammatory macrophage phenotype, and conditioned medium from treated tumor cells induced a similar macrophage reprogramming. In vivo , PFH-HIONs plus AMF inhibited tumor growth, increased necrosis, reduced Ki67, and were associated with increased intratumoral infiltration of CD8-positive lymphocyte-like cells and elevated IFN-γ levels, with acceptable short-term biosafety. PFH-HIONs function as a magnetothermal phase-transition nanoplatform with antitumor activity associated with ferroptosis, EMT suppression, and immune-related tumor microenvironment changes, supporting further investigation for image-guided breast cancer therapy.

title: Imageless Robot-assisted Lateral Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract: Background Lateral unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) is a technically demanding procedure because of the unique anatomy, biomechanics, and frequent posterolateral wear of the lateral compartment. Robotic assistance may improve accuracy and reproducibility. Purpose To describe a step-by-step technique for imageless robotic-assisted lateral UKA. Surgical technique The procedure is performed through a lateral parapatellar approach using the imageless CORI platform. Key steps include confirmation of isolated lateral osteoarthritis, imageless registration, dynamic ligament assessment, implant planning to address posterolateral wear while preserving constitutional valgus alignment, robotic bone preparation, and final implantation with assessment of alignment and ligament balance. Discussion Imageless robotic systems avoid preoperative CT imaging and enable real-time planning based on intraoperative soft-tissue assessment. These features may be particularly advantageous in lateral UKA. Conclusion Imageless robotic-assisted lateral UKA using the CORI system is a reproducible technique for isolated lateral compartment osteoarthritis. Accurate registration, preservation of native alignment, and dynamic assessment of ligament function are key principles for successful reconstruction.

title: Comparative efficacy of ultrasound versus elbow arthrography in treating Monteggia fractures in young children.
abstract: Purpose This study aims to compare the effectiveness and clinical value of ultrasound-assisted and arthrography-assisted treatment for acute Monteggia fractures in young children. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of 40 cases of acute Monteggia fractures in children treated with Kirschner wire or elastic intramedullary nail fixation between April 2020 and April 2025. Among these cases, 19 were treated under arthrography assistance (Group A), and 21 were treated under ultrasound guidance (Group B). We recorded baseline data for both groups, including gender, age, fracture side and type, associated injuries, time from injury to surgery, internal fixation device, fluoroscopy time, surgical duration, follow-up duration, and internal fixation removal time. Postoperative X-ray examination was performed to assess the quality of fracture reduction. Results Fluoroscopy time and surgical duration in Group B were significantly lower than in Group A (P < 0.05). Based on the evaluation criteria for assessing reduction quality, 17 cases were graded excellent, and 2 were considered good in Group A, while in Group B, 20 cases were deemed excellent and 1 was considered good. At the final follow-up, there was no significant difference in the range of elbow flexion, extension, pronation, and supination between the affected limbs of Group A and Group B (P > 0.05). Conclusion Ultrasound not only saves surgical time and reduces intraoperative radiation exposure for the patients but also enables the exploration of peripheral nerves, vessels, and soft tissue compressions.

title: Surgical versus Conservative Treatment of Isolated Posterior Malleolar Fractures: Clinical, Radiological, and Pedobarographic Outcomes.
abstract: Background Optimal management of isolated posterior malleolar (PM) fractures remains controversial, particularly regarding the influence of fracture fragment size on treatment selection and outcomes. Purpose To compare clinical, radiological, and pedobarographic outcomes of surgically and conservatively treated isolated PM fractures and to assess the effect of fracture fragment size on outcomes. Study design Retrospective observational study. Methods Patients with isolated PM fractures were divided into surgical and conservative groups. Fracture classification and fragment size were assessed using plain radiographs and computed tomography (CT). Clinical evaluation included the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score, visual analog scale (VAS) for pain, ankle range of motion, and radiographic osteoarthritis graded by the Kellgren-Lawrence classification. title: [The infected diabetic foot syndrome - diagnosis, treatment, and interdisciplinary care].
abstract: Abstract Diabetic foot syndrome (DFS) is one of the most severe long-term complications of diabetes mellitus and represents the leading cause of non-traumatic lower extremity amputations in industrialized nations. While the pathogenesis of foot ulcerations is primarily driven by a combination of diabetic polyneuropathy and peripheral arterial disease (PAD), secondary infections are frequently the main trigger for critical tissue loss. Consequently, these infections necessitate urgent inpatient admission and often result in major amputations as a last resort.The diagnosis of a diabetic foot infection is fundamentally based on clinical presentation. Key components for successful management include the early detection of underlying osteomyelitis, the identification of relevant perfusion deficits, and the immediate initiation of a structured, multimodal therapy regimen. This standard regimen comprises targeted surgical debridement, consistent pressure offloading, pathogen-specific antimicrobial therapy, and prompt vascular revascularization. Due to the highly complex underlying pathophysiology, patients with advanced disease stages benefit substantially from organized interdisciplinary care involving diabetologists, specialized podiatric surgeons, vascular surgeons, interventional radiologists, clinical infectious disease specialists, and orthopedic shoemakers. This comprehensive article provides a highly practice-oriented overview of the modern diagnosis and therapeutic management of the infected diabetic foot, strictly aligned with the current recommendations of the German Diabetes Society (DDG) and the International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF).

title: Prospective evaluation of deep-learning tools for the endoscopic detection of gastric precancerous conditions and eosinophilic esophagitis in a real-life cohort.
abstract: Background Neuronal-network-based methods have increasingly been applied to various tasks in gastrointestinal endoscopy, but prospective data are scarce. Recently, we published two Deep-Learning (DL) classifiers for the detection of gastric precancerous conditions (GPC) and eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE). Our aim was to investigate real-life performance of these tools in an unselected dataset of consecutive patients. Patients and methods In total, 650 patients undergoing esophagogastroduodenoscopy were recruited. Endoscopists selected up to six images in predefined scope positions (Loc 1-4 proximal stomach; Loc 5-6 esophagus) for evaluation. Finally, 1681 images of 583 patients were analyzed for GPC. For EoE, 936 images of 550 patients were analyzed. Results Among patients, 22/583 had GPC, and 7/550 presented with EoE. For the GPC classifier, there were many false positive predictions, especially for Loc2, whereas false negative tool predictions were relatively infrequent. The EoE tool showed fewer false positive results, false negative predictions were very uncommon. For both diseases the tool is better in avoiding false negative results while endoscopists were better in avoiding false positives. Conclusions Clinical utility of the GPC classifier is limited because of false predictions. When only using images from a single endoscopic standard position (Loc1), the algorithm performs satisfactorily. The performance of the EoE algorithm is more stable under real-life conditions.

title: [Cone beam CT-guided bronchoscopic navigation: step by step].
abstract: Abstract The assessment of peripheral lung lesions (PPH) is gaining increasing importance with the introduction of lung cancer screening using low-dose CT. Bronchoscopic navigation techniques, such as electromagnetic or virtual navigation bronchoscopy or robot-assisted bronchoscopy, are used for histological evaluation and have improved diagnostic accuracy. Navigation to the lesion using a preoperative chest CT scan can be inaccurate, particularly for small lesions or those in the lower lobe, due to CT-to-body divergence. Intraoperative 3D imaging using cone beam CT (CBCT) can significantly improve diagnostic accuracy. The combination of modern navigation techniques and CBCT is non-inferior to CT-guided transthoracic biopsy in terms of diagnostic accuracy and has a significantly more favorable risk profile. This article provides a detailed step-by-step description of how to perform CBCT-guided bronchoscopy.

title: Technology-Enabled Skin Longevity Optimization.
abstract: Aims and Backgrounds: Facial aging is a multifactorial process involving cellular senescence, ultraviolet damage, and structural decline across the epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous fat, and superficial musculoaponeurotic system. Contemporary rejuvenation has evolved beyond surgical repositioning toward biologically targeted cutaneous optimization. Technology Energy-based technologies including laser photothermolysis, radiofrequency-mediated dermal thermomodulation, microfocused ultrasound, and emerging microwave and cryobiologic modalities induce controlled tissue injury that activates wound-healing pathways, fibroblast proliferation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Techniques Regenerative strategies including microneedling-assisted mechanotransduction, platelet-derived biologics, autologous fat grafting, collagen biostimulators, and extracellular vesicle therapies provide biologically oriented tissue restoration through paracrine signaling and matrix synthesis. Current and Future Development: Artificial intelligence applications in facial phenotyping, treatment planning, and outcome assessment are emerging. Future directions include senescence-targeting therapies and precision-based multimodal protocols. Conclusions and clinical relevance Multimodal treatment sequencing addressing multiple anatomical layers represents the contemporary standard. Integration of device-based technologies with regenerative adjuncts enables biologically informed, individualized facial rejuvenation.

title: OVARIAN PRESERVATION IN PEDIATRIC OVARIAN TORSION: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW SUPPORTING DETORSION REGARDLESS OF TIMING OR INTRAOPERATIVE APPEARANCE.
abstract: Introduction One in five children with ovarian torsion undergo oophorectomy and/or salpingectomy. We sought to evaluate the current evidence regarding the timing of operative intervention, intraoperative decision making and postoperative follow-up in the management of pediatric ovarian torsion. Our goal is to optimize adnexal conservation in this population. Methods A systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42024605394) was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Mednar were searched for studies from 2010-2023 including pediatric patients (1-18 years) with benign ovarian torsion. Three clinical questions were addressed: (1) safe time window for operative detorsion based on symptom duration, (2) intraoperative findings guiding ovarian preservation, and (3) optimal timing of postoperative surveillance ultrasound. Results Of 1,035 screened studies, 19 met inclusion criteria (7 cohort studies, 12 case reports), with a total of 248 patients and 250 torsed ovaries. These studies were heterogenous in their reporting and overall have a level of evidence of 4. Ovarian conservation surgery was performed in 234/250 (94%) ovaries. Among those with documented follow-up (222/234, 95%), postoperative ultrasound demonstrated ovarian viability in 190/222 (86%). Delayed presentation and ischemic appearance did not reliably predict loss of function. Conclusion Ovarian conservation should be attempted in all cases of benign pediatric ovarian torsion, regardless of symptom duration or intraoperative appearance. Postoperative ultrasound within three months of detorsion is recommended to confirm ovarian viability and standardize follow-up care.

title: Knowledge, Compliance, and Associated Factors of Radiation Protection Adherence Among Dental Students, Interns, and Dentists: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Objectives Dental radiography is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning, but exposure to ionizing radiation requires strict adherence to radiation protection principles. This study evaluated radiation protection knowledge, self-reported compliance, and their associated factors among dental students, interns, and dentists. Materials and methods A cross-sectional study included 136 participants (86.1% response rate). A content-reviewed bilingual questionnaire assessed 7 knowledge items (6 scored in the composite knowledge score) and 12 self-reported compliance items. Pilot testing, translation, content validity (scale-level average content validity index [S-CVI/Ave] = 0.91), and internal consistency (α = 0.78; Kuder-Richardson Formula 20 [KR-20] = 0.70) were evaluated. Multivariable ordinary least squares regression examined factors associated with compliance using SPSS 27 and Python software. Results The composite knowledge score was 0.804; the pediatric radiation protection item had a correct-response rate of 54.4% (single-item assessment). Mean compliance was 3.09/4. Composite knowledge score was independently associated with self-reported compliance ( B = 1.092, 95% confidence interval: 0.817-1.366, p < 0.001). Compliance was significantly lower among Year 5 students and interns than among Year 3 students ( p = 0.037 and p = 0.005, respectively), whereas gender and the remaining training-level contrasts were not significant ( R 2 = 0.360). Knowledge showed a moderate-to-strong positive correlation with compliance ( rₛ = 0.528, p < 0.001). Exploratory analyses indicated a stronger knowledge-compliance association among more advanced trainees (Year 5, interns, and dentists/faculty) than among earlier-year students. The largest compliance gaps involved X-ray image repetition frequency, use of protective shielding devices, and motion-restraining tools. Conclusion Composite knowledge score was independently associated with self-reported compliance, and adjusted compliance was lower among Year 5 students and interns than among Year 3 students. However, the cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported data preclude causal interpretation. Lower compliance was observed for X-ray image repetition frequency, protective shielding devices, and motion-restraining tools. These findings support competency-based training and curriculum review, but recommendations remain exploratory and require confirmation in larger multi-institutional prospective studies.

title: Radiographic manifestations of pneumatosis intestinalis and construction of an AI-assisted diagnostic system.
abstract: Pneumatosis intestinalis (PI) has a wide range of etiologies, and the imaging differentiation between benign and ischemic PI is difficult, leading to a high risk of missed diagnosis. This study systematically summarizes the CT (Computed Tomography) imaging manifestations of PI and constructs an AI (Artificial Intelligence)-assisted diagnostic model that integrates multidimensional features. This study retrospectively collected CT and x-ray data from 612 patients with PI (398 benign and 214 ischemic cases) from three tertiary hospitals, and included an external validation set of 106 cases. Imaging analysis established a five-level PI-CT severity scoring system based on gas morphology, distribution, portal venous gas (PVG), intestinal wall enhancement, mesenteric edema, and ascites. The AI system adopted a two-level architecture: The first level used EfficientNet-B3 for rapid screening on x-ray films; the second level used 3D nnU-Net (No-new-Net) to segment intestinal wall gas, and then fused the data through a three-branch network (gas morphology, accompanying signs, and clinical metadata) via cross-attention to output the probability of ischemic PI. In the internal test set, the model achieved an AUC (Area Under the Curve) of 0.947 for ischemic PI (sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 93.6%), significantly outperforming senior radiologists (AUC = 0.876); the AUC on the external validation set was 0.931. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis showed that PVG and blood lactate were the most important predictors. This two-tiered AI system can significantly improve the early identification of the causes of critical PI, providing a reliable method for intelligent diagnosis of emergency imaging.

This study retrospectively collected CT and x-ray data from 612 patients with PI (398 benign and 214 ischemic cases) from three tertiary hospitals, and included an external validation set of 106 cases. Imaging analysis established a five-level PI-CT severity scoring system based on gas morphology, distribution, portal venous gas (PVG), intestinal wall enhancement, mesenteric edema, and ascites. The AI system adopted a two-level architecture: The first level used EfficientNet-B3 for rapid screening on x-ray films; the second level used 3D nnU-Net (No-new-Net) to segment intestinal wall gas, and then fused the data through a three-branch network (gas morphology, accompanying signs, and clinical metadata) via cross-attention to output the probability of ischemic PI. In the internal test set, the model achieved an AUC (Area Under the Curve) of 0.947 for ischemic PI (sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 93.6%), significantly outperforming senior radiologists (AUC = 0.876); the AUC on the external validation set was 0.931. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis showed that PVG and blood lactate were the most important predictors. This two-tiered AI system can significantly improve the early identification of the causes of critical PI, providing a reliable method for intelligent diagnosis of emergency imaging.

title: Foundation models in radiology: Development, applications, and future impact.
abstract: Foundation models represent a major evolution in artificial intelligence, enabling models pretrained on large, diverse datasets to be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks with substantially less task-specific training data. In radiology, advances in transformer architectures, self-supervised learning, and vision-language models have created new opportunities to integrate image and text understanding within versatile artificial intelligence systems. Potential applications span the radiology workflow and include image interpretation, automated report drafting and summarization, clinical decision support, information retrieval, and development of specialized task-specific models. Among these, AI-assisted report generation represents a particularly promising near-term application, although current performance supports a role as a drafting assistant rather than an autonomous replacement for radiologists. Important barriers to clinical adoption remain, including limitations in model performance, regulatory requirements, and the risk of automation bias. In the near term, foundation models may have their greatest impact by augmenting radiologists and accelerating the development of specialized artificial intelligence applications rather than replacing existing systems or physician expertise. This review describes the technological advances underlying foundation models, highlights their current and emerging applications in radiology, examines key risks and implementation challenges, and considers their potential impact on the future practice of radiology.

title: The impact of artificial intelligence on peer review in radiology journals.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming radiology research and is progressively influencing the scholarly publication process itself. Large language models (LLMs) are being increasingly used for manuscript writing. At the other end of the spectrum, AI can assist with manuscript screening, statistical and methodological assessment, language editing, reference checking, reviewer selection, and the generation of peer-review comments. LLMs have the potential to improve the efficiency of journal review by reducing repetitive tasks and helping reviewers identify reporting deficiencies. However, their integration also introduces substantial concerns regarding confidentiality, hallucination, bias, reproducibility, authorship, accountability, and manipulation of the peer-review process. In this article, the authors examine the potential benefits and limitations of AI-assisted peer review in radiology journals and propose a framework in which AI serves as a controlled decision-support tool rather than an autonomous reviewer. Human reviewers and editors should retain responsibility for scientific judgment, confidentiality, and final editorial decisions. This approach harnesses AI's efficiency while maintaining accountability.

title: Should the carbon footprint of imaging be considered to ensure an effective, sustainable supplementary breast screening strategy for women with dense breasts?
abstract: Breast density is an independent risk factor for breast cancer and reduces the sensitivity of mammography, increasing the chance of a missed breast cancer. Notifying women of their breast density aims to increase their awareness about their breast cancer risk and support discussions about supplemental screening (e.g. ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging) with their healthcare providers. Although supplemental screening may improve cancer detection, it also brings challenges, including lack of international consensus on how best to manage screening in women with dense breasts. The implementation of breast density notification and supplemental screening will significantly impact global screening programs, and provides an opportunity to re-evaluate screening pathways, not only in terms of benefits and harms, but also environmental sustainability. In this perspective, we discuss the benefits and harms of supplemental screening for women with dense breasts, including the carbon footprint of screening, and considerations for clinicians, consumers and policymakers.

title: Clinical and behavioral delineation of cochlear implant non-users: a 20-year retrospective descriptive analysis.
abstract: Background Although cochlear implants (CIs) effectively restore hearing, device abandonment ('non-use') remains a critical challenge limiting long-term auditory rehabilitation. Aims/objectives This study aimed to evaluate the prevalence, clinical and radiological characteristics, and patient-reported reasons for CI non-use, comparing pre-lingually and post-lingually deafened individuals to inform long-term retention strategies. Material and methods We retrospectively reviewed 545 CI recipients implanted between 2002 and 2023 (excluding 24 patients lost to follow-up or with incomplete data). Clinical features, temporal bone CT, internal auditory canal MRI, and speech-language therapy records of 36 non-users were analyzed. Results Overall non-use rate was 6.6% (36/545), comprising 8.7% (25/287) in pre-lingual and 4.3% (11/258) in post-lingual recipients. Inner ear anomalies were identified in 11 pre-lingual non-users, including two with isolated cochlear nerve deficiency. Primary non-use reasons were sound maladaptation (48.0% pre-lingual vs. 36.4% post-lingual) and lack of subjective listening effect (48.0% vs. 18.2%). Post-lingual non-users presented distinct adult-specific psychosocial barriers (27.3%), including depression and cognitive decline. Conclusions and significance CI non-use is driven by distinct physiological, psychological, and socioeconomic factors depending on deafness onset. Delineating these onset-specific profiles provides essential guidance for tailored preoperative counseling and age-appropriate post-implantation monitoring to minimize long-term device abandonment.

title: Association of second-trimester maternal serum AFP with umbilical venous blood flow and placental morphometry: a prospective study.
abstract: Background Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and umbilical venous Doppler measurements may reflect different aspects of fetoplacental function, but their relationship during the second trimester remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate associations between maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein multiples of the median (AFP MoM) and umbilical venous Doppler parameters, foetal weight percentile, and placental morphometry. Methods This prospective observational study included 104 singleton pregnancies examined at 16-22 weeks. Maternal blood sampling and ultrasound/Doppler assessment were performed on the same day. Associations were evaluated using Spearman correlations and partial Spearman correlations adjusted for gestational age. Exploratory comparisons between pregnancies with AFP <2.0 MoM and AFP ≥2.0 MoM were also adjusted for gestational age. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure controlled the false discovery rate. Results AFP MoM was available for 103 pregnancies and was not associated with foetal weight percentile or umbilical venous Doppler parameters. A weak inverse association with placental length was observed after gestational-age adjustment (partial r = -0.229; nominal p = 0.021), but it did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction ( p = 0.193). In the exploratory analysis, the AFP ≥2.0 MoM group had a lower adjusted placental length (difference, -11.63 mm; 95% confidence interval, -21.10 to -2.17; nominal p = 0.017), but this difference was not significant after correction ( p = 0.149). Conclusion Maternal serum AFP MoM was not associated with contemporaneous umbilical venous Doppler parameters or foetal weight percentile. Findings involving placental length were weak and should be considered exploratory.

title: CosMxScope: scalable reconstruction and digital pathology integration of imaging-based CosMx spatial transcriptomics data.
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics technologies have transformed the capacity to quantify gene expression from human tissues, simultaneously capturing both the cell functional state and spatial organization at cellular and subcellular resolution. The CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager (SMI) is one of the leading platforms at single-cell spatial multi-modal omics profiling, capable of measuring thousands of RNA or protein targets at single-cell and subcellular resolution across whole slide sections. Exported data include field-of-view (FOV) image tiles, subcellular transcript coordinates, and cell segmentation polygons, outputs that are rich in spatial information but not directly compatible with widely used digital pathology tools. Here we present CosMxScope, a lightweight open-source Python framework designed for data exported from the CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager through the AtoMx platform, bridging CosMx spatial outputs with histopathology visualization environments. CosMxScope provides functions for stitching FOV image tiles into reconstructed whole-slide images, converting cell segmentation polygons and transcript coordinates into GeoJSON objects for downstream visualization and assessment within QuPath, and generating spatial visualization plots of cell types, transcript locations, and gene expression patterns. The framework is designed for practical use in translational research settings, enabling interactive exploration of spatial transcriptomic data alongside cell morphology. CosMxScope has been applied in multiple ongoing research projects involving CosMx profiling of human and mouse tissues, supporting pathology-based spatial analysis workflows. This open-source software is available at https://github.com/AivaraX-AI/CosMxScope.

title: Exoscope-assisted resection of spinal tumors: volumetric efficacy, safety and learning curve analysis in 47 consecutive cases.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the clinical outcomes, volumetric extent of resection, safety profile, and skill acquisition dynamics of 3D-4K digital exoscope-assisted spinal tumor resection. Methods A retrospective analytical single-center study was conducted on 47 consecutive patients undergoing exoscope-assisted resection across intramedullary (IM, n = 7), intradural extramedullary (IDEM, n = 34), and extradural (ED, n = 6) compartments. Extent of resection was determined via blinded postoperative subtraction MRI. Surgical skill acquisition was modeled using sequential Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) analysis of intraoperative blood loss. Results Mean age was 49.1 ± 17.3 years (63.8% female). Overall Gross Total Resection (GTR > 95%) was achieved in 85.1% ( n = 40/47), reaching 100% in IM lesions ( n = 7/7) and 82.4% in IDEM tumors ( n = 28/34, p = 0.567). Postoperative CSF fistula occurred in 6.4% ( n = 3/47), restricted exclusively to IDEM Schwannomas. Median operative time was 3.27 hours (IQR: 2.68-5.05; n = 32/47). Median hospital stay was 3.0 days (IQR: 3.0-5.0). At 6-month follow-up, paired evaluations demonstrated significant functional and pain improvements (mMs and ODI/NDI, p < 0.001). Sequential CUSUM analysis identified a structural break at case 28, marking the transition to technical mastery without blood loss inflation during early cases ( p = 0.553). Conclusions Resection of spinal tumors using the 3D-4K exoscope is safe, effective, and yields high volumetric resection rates. Skill acquisition follows a patient-safe learning curve, achieving technical proficiency at case 28.

title: Hyper-acute orbital edema and vision loss following palliative radiotherapy of the lacrimal gland.
abstract: Breast carcinoma is the most common primary malignancy to metastasize to the orbit. While mild delayed orbital edema is a recognized complication of orbital radiotherapy, hyper-acute severe edema resulting in transient vision loss is rare. A 48-year-old woman with metastatic invasive lobular breast carcinoma and left orbital involvement received a first-dose palliative radiation fraction of 8 Gy to the left orbit. Within 5 hours, she developed severe proptosis, chemosis, elevated intraocular pressure, and monocular vision loss. Computed tomography demonstrated proptosis of the left globe and optic nerve stretching. She received 8 mg of intravenous dexamethasone, and her vision rapidly recovered to baseline with the resolution of her acute compressive symptoms without any change in tumor-directed therapy. This case highlights the rare risk of hyper-acute post-radiation orbital edema within hours of radiotherapy and demonstrates that early, prompt medical management can successfully rescue compressive optic neuropathy.

title: A multicenter large-sample survey on adverse events of focused ultrasound ablation surgery for benign uterine diseases in clinical training and teaching hospitals.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the adverse events and complications associated with focused ultrasound ablation surgery(FUAS)for benign uterine diseases in teaching and training centers. Materials and methods From October 2010 to December 2023, 26,844 patients with benign uterine diseases were treated with FUAS and more than 2000 doctors had been trained in three teaching and training centers. Among the treated patients, 16,619 had uterine fibroids, 8732 had adenomyosis, 1154 had cesarean scar pregnancy, and 379 had placental accreta spectrum. According to the classification system of the Society of Interventional Radiology (SIR), these adverse events were classified as mild adverse event (no therapy or nominal therapy), moderate adverse event (moderate escalation of care, requiring substantial treatment), severe adverse event (marked escalation of care), Life-threatening or disabling event, and patient death or unexpected pregnancy abortion. Results Mild adverse effects occurred in 2,352 (8.75%) patients, moderate adverse events were seen in 147 (0.55%) patients, severe adverse events encountered in 50 (0.18%) patients. No life-threatening or disabling event, and patient death or unexpected pregnancy abortion occurred. The overall incidence rate of severe adverse events was 0.18% ( n = 50). From 2010 to 2023, the annual incidence rates of severe adverse events were 0%, 0.42%, 0%, 0%, 0.28%, 0.23%, 0.09%, 0.08%, 0.20%, 0.28%, 0.44%, 0.16%, 0.16%, and 0.10%, respectively. Conclusion Based on the results, we concluded that FUAS is a safe treatment for benign uterine diseases. The training course for trainee did not increase the risk of severe adverse events.

Mild adverse effects occurred in 2,352 (8.75%) patients, moderate adverse events were seen in 147 (0.55%) patients, severe adverse events encountered in 50 (0.18%) patients. No life-threatening or disabling event, and patient death or unexpected pregnancy abortion occurred. The overall incidence rate of severe adverse events was 0.18% (n = 50). From 2010 to 2023, the annual incidence rates of severe adverse events were 0%, 0.42%, 0%, 0%, 0.28%, 0.23%, 0.09%, 0.08%, 0.20%, 0.28%, 0.44%, 0.16%, 0.16%, and 0.10%, respectively.

Conclusion

Based on the results, we concluded that FUAS is a safe treatment for benign uterine diseases. The training course for trainee did not increase the risk of severe adverse events.

title: Long-term outcomes of LINAC single-dose versus fractionated stereotactic radiation for vestibular schwannoma.
abstract: Introduction Vestibular schwannomas (VS) are increasingly being managed with LINAC-based stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) or fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy (fSRT). There is a paucity of long-term outcomes especially in relation to post-treatment volumetric tumour and pseudoprogression data. Methods 197 patients treated with LINAC-SRS ( n = 92) and LINAC-fSRT ( n = 105) between November 2003 and September 2019 were analysed. Tumour control was assessed volumetrically using MRI. The primary outcome was radiological VS control at last follow-up. The secondary outcomes were freedom from further intervention, serviceable hearing at last follow-up and incidence of new or worsened facial nerve palsy. Results Patients undergoing fSRT had larger pre-treatment tumour size (2.1 cm 3 vs 1.0, p = 0.008). At a median follow-up of 10.9 years, radiological control rates were 94% for SRS and 91% for fSRT (p = 0.41). Rates of freedom from further surgical or radiation intervention were 98% and 97%, respectively. SRS showed a larger median pseudoprogression (≈75%). Facial nerve palsy and sensation changes were low and comparable between the groups. Hydrocephalus occurred more frequently after fSRT (9.8% vs. 1.1%, p = 0.021). Conclusion LINAC-fSRT and LINAC-SRS are both associated with excellent long-term tumour control rates. Hydrocephalus was more common in patients after fSRT with the caveat these patients had a larger pre-treatment tumour volume.

title: Association of HIV infection with short-term major adverse cardiovascular events among Chinese patients with carotid atherosclerosis: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Background People living with HIV (PLWH) suffer accelerated atherosclerotic injury, but real-world Chinese cohort data excluding patients with pre-existing cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases remain scarce regarding HIV-related incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). This study aimed to explore the independent associations between HIV infection and 2-year incident MACE among Chinese patients with carotid atherosclerosis free of prior cardiovascular events, and identify correlated metabolic and renal factors. Methods A retrospective single-center cohort design was adopted. We enrolled patients with ultrasound-confirmed carotid atherosclerosis from January 2020 to June 2023, excluded individuals with prior coronary heart disease, ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, and conducted standardized 2-year follow-up for all eligible participants. Univariate statistical tests screened variables correlated with MACE; variables with univariate p < 0.05 plus core clinical confounders (age, sex, hypertension, diabetes) were incorporated into multivariate binary logistic regression to identify independent correlates of new-onset MACE. Results Patients with HIV infection showed significantly younger age compared with HIV-negative counterparts (63.55 ± 10.81 years vs 70.61 ± 9.75 years, p < 0.001). The cumulative 2-year occurrence rate of MACE was markedly higher in the HIV-positive group (40.4% versus 22.9%, p = 0.023). Multivariate regression analysis verified four independent risk markers for incident MACE: HIV seropositivity (OR = 2.24, 95%CI 1.19-4.22, p = 0.012), baseline active smoking (OR = 1.98, 95%CI 1.07-3.66, p = 0.028), reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) (OR = 2.15, 95%CI 1.15-4.02, p = 0.017) and hyperuricemia (OR = 1.89, 95%CI 1.02-3.51, p = 0.043). Conclusion Chinese people living with HIV (PLWH) combined with carotid atherosclerosis develop atherosclerotic lesions at an earlier age and carry elevated short-term MACE risk. Integrated intervention strategies covering HIV viral control, smoking cessation, renal function protection and serum uric acid management can effectively improve cardiovascular long-term prognosis for this special population.

title: Association between pancreatic ectopic fat deposition and QCT-assessed bone mass status in patients with chronic kidney disease: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: Background Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at increased risk of bone abnormalities. Beyond disturbances in mineral metabolism, ectopic fat deposition may also be associated with skeletal abnormalities in CKD. However, the relationship between pancreatic fat and bone mass status remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the association between mean pancreatic fat fraction and quantitative computed tomography (QCT)-assessed bone mass status in patients with CKD. Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included 327 patients with CKD. Vertebral volumetric bone mineral density was measured using QCT to classify bone mass status as normal bone mass, osteopenia, or osteoporosis. Mean pancreatic fat fraction was quantified from CT images. Ordinal logistic regression, restricted cubic spline (RCS), subgroup analyses, and sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate its association with bone mass status. Results Mean pancreatic fat fraction was highest in patients with osteoporosis ( p < 0.001). In the fully adjusted model, each 5-percentage-point increase in mean pancreatic fat fraction was associated with higher odds of a more severe bone mass category (OR = 1.481, 95% CI: 1.152-1.905, p = 0.002). RCS analysis showed a significant overall association ( p = 0.009), with no evidence of nonlinearity ( p = 0.290). No statistically significant interactions were detected for sex, age, diabetes status, or CKD stage. Conclusion A higher mean pancreatic fat fraction was associated with more severe bone mass categories in patients with CKD after adjustment for the measured covariates. QCT-based pancreatic fat assessment may provide additional information on metabolic features associated with bone mass abnormalities in CKD.

title: Nonverbal reasoning in children and adolescents with cerebral palsy: associations with gross motor function, MRI, and EEG findings.
abstract: To examine the association between gross motor function level and Raven's Colored Progressive Matrices (CPM) performance in children and adolescents with cerebral palsy (CP), compare CPM performance with typically developing participants, and explore associations with MRI and EEG findings. This multicenter cross-sectional study included 40 participants with CP and 20 comparison participants aged 10-17 years. CPM totals were converted to center-derived age-referenced scores; the upper available normative age band was applied above age 11.5 years. Gross motor function was classified with the GMFCS. Clinically indicated MRI and EEG findings were categorized using prespecified systems. Median CPM score was 72 (IQR 64-81) in the CP group and 98 (IQR 92-104) in the comparison group (adjusted difference -26.4, 95% CI -31.2 to -21.6). GMFCS level was inversely associated with CPM score (Spearman rho = -.78, 95% CI -.85 to -.68). Predominant white matter injury was associated with lower CPM scores. The adjusted association with epileptiform EEG abnormalities was inconclusive. CPM performance was associated with GMFCS level and MRI pattern, but the cross-sectional findings do not establish causality. Gross motor classification must not substitute for accessible neuropsychological assessment.

title: Schizophrenia heterogeneity, treatment response to clozapine, and the Johns Hopkins Schizoaffective Disorders Precision Medicine Center of Excellence.
abstract: Schizophrenia heterogeneity has resisted resolution for over a century, with no unifying clinical feature, biomarker, or pathogenic pathway identified. This has produced imprecise diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment, while confounding mechanistic research. Prior subtyping approaches-based on clinical phenotype, longitudinal course, age of onset, neuroimaging, physiological measures, or etiological factors-have yielded partial insights but lack established clinical utility. The Johns Hopkins Schizoaffective Disorder Precision Medicine Center of Excellence (PMCOE) brings together patients and clinicians at the Johns Hopkins Hospital and the Johns Hopkins Bayview Community Psychiatry Program with Johns Hopkins schizophrenia investigators to address this heterogeneity through stratification by treatment response, dividing patients into non-treatment-resistant (nonTRS), clozapine-responsive treatment-resistant (crTRS), and ultra-treatment-resistant (uTRS) subgroups. The term "Schizoaffective Disorder" was chosen to include schizophrenia with varying degrees of affective symptomatology, deliberately creating a broadly inclusive patient group. We hypothesize that these subtypes reflect distinct pathophysiological processes and that identifying their biological correlates will improve clinical decision-making and reveal novel therapeutic targets. The PMCOE pursues this hypothesis across four aims. Aim 1 characterizes clinical, cognitive, functional, quality-of-life, and olfactory signatures distinguishing subtypes, with preliminary data showing worse cognition and function in uTRS versus crTRS, and a temporal sequence of clozapine benefit (symptoms, then function, then quality of life). Aim 2 applies 7T structural/functional MRI-including novel measures of microvascular perfusion (iVASO) and CSF clearance (cDSC)-alongside EEG-based dynamic causal and network modeling to probe excitatory/inhibitory imbalance across subtypes. Aim 3 investigates cellular and molecular mechanisms, particularly protein homeostasis dysfunction, using patient-derived induced neurons, organoids, and extracellular vesicles, with focused study of SCHEMA-identified risk genes, including CUL1. Aim 4 leverages electronic health record data to generate validated electronic phenotypes for treatment-response subtypes and to establish a learning health system translating findings into clinical practice. By anchoring subtyping to an empirically measurable, clinically actionable outcome, the PMCOE aims to accelerate biomarker discovery for clozapine response, clarify mechanisms of treatment resistance, and transform care for individuals with schizophrenia-particularly those with ultra-treatment-resistant illness, for whom therapeutic options remain critically limited.

title: Non-invasive vascular assessment in gestational hypertension and preeclampsia during pregnancy and the postpartum period: a systematic review.
abstract: Objective To evaluate evidence on non-invasive vascular assessment techniques used during pregnancy and/or the postpartum period to identify vascular abnormalities associated with gestational hypertension and explore potential implications for long-term cardiovascular health. Methods A systematic search of MEDLINE, PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, and gray literature (to May-2024) identified studies assessing vascular structure or function using pulse-wave velocity, carotid intima-media thickness, flow-mediated dilation, ophthalmic artery Doppler, and retinal imaging. Forty-nine studies involving 32,683 participants. Due to the heterogeneity in study design and methodology, findings were synthesized narratively. Results Women with gestational hypertension generally demonstrated increased arterial stiffness (elevated pulse wave velocity and augmentation index), impaired endothelial function (reduced flow-mediated dilation), and increased intima-media thickness during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Several studies reported persistence of these abnormalities from weeks to years after delivery, although findings were inconsistent. Ophthalmic artery Doppler studies showed variable alterations in peak systolic velocity ratios and pulsatility index reported in hypertensive pregnancies. Retinal imaging identified alterations in retinal vessel caliber during pregnancy and the postpartum period, with some abnormalities reported up to six years postpartum. Conclusion Non-invasive vascular assessments can help identify macrovascular, microvascular, and endothelial abnormalities in women with gestational hypertension and preeclampsia during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Although some abnormalities persist beyond delivery and may contribute to long-term cardiovascular risk, evidence remains insufficient to support their use as independent predictors of future cardiovascular events. Further standardized, prospective longitudinal studies are needed to determine their prognostic and clinical value.

title: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Circulatory Arrest - A Joint Position Statement and Resource Document of NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP, and AAP.
abstract: In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest. NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend:EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should:Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician's scope of practice. These include:External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquetsAirway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empiric bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. title: Factors associated with mammography screening stages in Hispanic/Latina women in the USA: a transtheoretical model and health belief model approach.
abstract: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among Hispanic/Latina women in the U.S. and they are more likely to be diagnosed at later stages. Understanding psychosocial factors associated with mammography screening is important for addressing these disparities. This study examined associations between Transtheoretical Model (TTM) stages of mammography screening and constructs from the Health Belief Model (HBM) and TTM, including self-efficacy, perceived benefits, barriers, susceptibility, and seriousness, as well as family support, among Hispanic/Latina women aged 40 years and older in the U.S.A. A cross-sectional design using self-report surveys was employed, with 473 Hispanic/Latina women recruited through multiple nonprobability sampling strategies. A one-way ANCOVA compared psychosocial factors across the three combined TTM groups (precontemplation/contemplation/preparation, relapse/inconsistent, maintenance), controlling for age. Statistically significant differences were found among the three combined TTM groups for self-efficacy (F(2, 469) = 13.08, p = 0.000), benefits (F(2, 469) = 5.21, p = 0.006), barriers (F(2, 469) = 6.90, p = 0.001), susceptibility (F(2, 469) = 8.37, p = 0.000), seriousness (F(2, 469) = 4.64, p = 0.01), and family support (F(2, 469) = 10.34, p = 0.000). These significant differences across the three combined TTM groups highlight the multifaceted nature of mammography screening behavior. Family support, often underrepresented in traditional health behavior models, was also associated with the combined TTM groups. In this study, family support was primarily reflected in family-related health communication and advice. These findings suggest that using the HBM and TTM as complementary frameworks, alongside family support, may inform culturally tailored interventions addressing individual beliefs and familial contexts to promote regular mammography screening among Hispanic/Latina women. Future longitudinal research should examine these factors across Hispanic/Latina subgroups and settings to better understand their relationships with mammography screening and inform targeted health promotion strategies.

title: Efficacy of hysteroscopic curettage and niche resection in type II and III cesarean scar pregnancies.
abstract: Introduction To evaluate the efficacy and safety of hysteroscopic curettage combined with cesarean scar diverticulum canal-opening after focused ultrasound ablation surgery (FUAS) pretreatment in patients with type II and III cesarean scar pregnancy (CSP). Methods Clinical data of 105 patients with type II/III CSP treated between January 2019 and October 2022 were retrospectively analyzed. All patients received FUAS pretreatment. The observation group ( n = 47) underwent hysteroscopic curettage combined with niche canal-opening, while the control group ( n = 58) received hysteroscopic curettage alone. Surgical parameters, postoperative recovery, complications, reintervention rates, and menstrual outcomes were compared. Results The observation group had significantly shorter operation time [20 (15,25) vs. 25 (20,31) min, p = 0.001], less intraoperative blood loss [5 (5,10) vs. 10 (10,50) mL, p = 0.002], lower complication rate [4.3% vs. 17.2%, p = 0.038], and lower reintervention rate [4.3% vs. 19.0%, p = 0.023]. No between-group differences were observed in postoperative hemoglobin decline, hospital stay, vaginal bleeding duration, human chorionic gonadotropin normalization time, menstrual recovery time, or residual scar myometrial thickness (all p > 0.05). Among patients with preoperative prolonged menstruation, menstrual duration improved in both groups ( p < 0.05), with a higher improvement rate in the observation group [75.0% vs. 23.1%, p = 0.005]. Conclusions FUAS pretreatment combined with hysteroscopic surgery is safe and effective for type II/III CSP. Adding diverticulum canal-opening to hysteroscopic curettage further optimized surgical outcomes by reducing operation time, intraoperative blood loss, complication rates, and the need for reintervention, while also significantly improving prolonged menstruation. This combined strategy may serve as an optimized minimally invasive alternative for patients desiring fertility, though long-term reproductive safety requires further verification.

title: Diagnostic performance of MRI, endorectal ultrasound, and FAPI PET/MRI for identifying pathological complete response after short-course radiotherapy and chemoimmunotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer: a retrospective study.
abstract: Background Accurate imaging-based response assessment is essential for proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of MRI, endorectal ultrasound (ERUS) and 18F-FAPI PET/MRI for identifying pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy (SCRT) followed by chemoimmunotherapy. Methods This single-center retrospective study included 143 patients. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy with 95% confidence intervals. Cohen's κ assessed agreement between imaging-defined complete response (iCR) and pCR. Paired comparisons used Cochran's Q and Holm-adjusted exact McNemar tests. Results The pCR rate was 51.0%. MRI ( n = 118), ERUS ( n = 81), and PET/MRI ( n = 25) achieved sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 4.76%, 98.18%, and 48.31%; 30.95%, 87.18%, and 58.02%; and 60.0%, 100.0%, and 84.0%, respectively. PET/MRI-assessed imaging complete response showed substantial agreement with pCR (κ = 0.643). Conclusion Neoadjuvant SCRT followed by chemoimmunotherapy achieved high pCR rates in pMMR LARC. Conventional MRI and ERUS showed limited sensitivity despite relatively high specificity. 18F-FAPI PET/MRI showed potential diagnostic utility in a small subgroup, but its moderate sensitivity and limited sample size warrant further validation. These findings highlight the limitations of imaging alone and the need for comprehensive response assessment.

title: Combined radiofrequency electromagnetic and pulsed magnetic field exposure attenuates histological and molecular markers of acute colonic injury in young rats.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease involves epithelial injury, ulceration, apoptosis, inflammation, and oxidative-stress dysregulation. Although bioelectromagnetic fields may modulate tissue responses, their effects on acute colitis remain unclear. This exploratory study assessed histological and molecular changes associated with combined radiofrequency electromagnetic field (RF-EMF) and pulsed magnetic field (PMF) exposure in acetic-acid-induced colitis.Thirty-two young female Wistar albino rats were allocated to Control, Colitis, Colitis+RF-EMF+PMF, or RF-EMF+PMF groups (n=8 each). Colitis was induced intrarectally with 4% acetic acid. Exposure comprised RF-EMF (27.12 MHz, 30 min/session, 12 cycles/day) and PMF (0.5 mT, continuous). After seven days, distal colonic specimens underwent semiquantitative histopathology, crypt morphometry, immunohistochemistry for CAS-3, IL-6, and TNF-α, and RT-qPCR for SIRT-1, NRF-2, and HO-1. Colitis caused histological injury, reduced crypt dimensions, increased CAS-3, IL-6, and TNF-α immunopositivity, and decreased SIRT-1, NRF-2, and HO-1 expression. Compared with untreated colitis, combined exposure increased crypt depth and width and reduced all three immunohistochemical markers (all Tukey-adjusted p<0.001). Overall histopathological injury was lower but not statistically significant (Dunn-adjusted p=0.068), whereas submucosal inflammatory infiltration decreased significantly (p=0.048). NRF-2 expression increased (Tukey-adjusted p=0.002); SIRT-1 and HO-1 increased numerically without statistical significance (p=0.057 and 0.134).Combined RF-EMF+PMF exposure was associated with preserved crypt architecture, reduced apoptotic and inflammatory immunopositivity, and increased NRF-2 expression. Absent barrier-function testing and incomplete RF dosimetry preclude conclusions regarding restored epithelial barrier function or established therapeutic efficacy.

title: Targeting Accelerated Aging in COPD: The AMICO (A Trial of Metformin In COpd) Trial Design.
abstract: Introduction Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is increasingly recognized as a disease of accelerated biological aging characterized by progressive lung function decline, emphysema progression and multiple age-related comorbidities. Current therapies improve symptoms and reduce exacerbations but have limited effects on disease progression. Metformin has demonstrated anti-aging properties through modulation of pathways involved in oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular senescence, making it a potential disease-modifying treatment in COPD. Methods AMICO (A Trial of Metformin In COPD) is an investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial conducted in anonymous . A total of 212 patients with clinically stable COPD, centrilobular emphysema on computed tomography, post-bronchodilator FEV 1 40%-70% predicted and accelerated FEV 1 decline (>40 mL·year -1 ) will be randomized (1:1) to receive metformin (850 mg twice daily) or matching placebo for 36 months in addition to standard COPD treatment. Assessments include pulmonary function, chest computed tomography, exercise capacity, health status, muscle strength, body composition, age associated comorbidities development and aging-related biomarkers.The primary endpoint is the annual rate of FEV 1 decline over 36 months. Secondary endpoints include emphysema progression, changes in diffusing capacity, COPD Assessment Test score, 6-minute walk distance, BODE index, handgrip strength, exacerbations, major cardiovascular events, cancer incidence and renal dysfunction. Conclusions AMICO is the first randomized trial specifically designed to evaluate metformin as a gerotherapeutic and disease-modifying intervention in COPD. The study may provide novel evidence supporting geroscience-based approaches to slow disease progression and improve long-term outcomes in patients with COPD.

title: The FOXA2-BNIP3 axis alleviates acute necrotizing pancreatitis by promoting mitophagy in pancreatic acinar cells to inhibit mtDNA-mediated AIM2 inflammasome activation.
abstract: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis (ANP) is a severe inflammatory pancreatic disease characterized by pancreatic necrosis and systemic inflammation, with complex pathogenesis, rapid progression, and poor prognosis. Mitochondrial dysfunction in pancreatic acinar cells represents a pivotal early event in ANP; however, mitophagy, a central component of mitochondrial quality control, remains poorly characterized in terms of its role, regulatory networks, and therapeutic potential in ANP. In this study, we demonstrated that BNIP3 (BCL2 interacting protein 3) expression was significantly downregulated in patients with ANP and negatively correlated with inflammatory severity. Consistently, BNIP3-mediated mitophagy was impaired in the pancreatic tissue of ANP mouse models. Notably, restoration of BNIP3 expression using a novel adeno-associated virus targeting pancreatic tissue (AAV-PAN)- Bnip3 gene therapy vector alleviated pancreatic necrosis and systemic inflammatory injury, promoted mitophagy, and inhibited mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Mechanistically, BNIP3-dependent mitophagy facilitated the clearance of damaged mitochondria and prevented mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release into the cytosol, thereby suppressing AIM2 (absent in melanoma 2) inflammasome activation and subsequent acinar cell pyroptosis. Furthermore, we identified the transcription factor FOXA2 (forkhead box A2) as a direct upstream regulator that bound to the Bnip3 promoter and positively regulated its expression. FOXA2 was downregulated in ANP, whereas pancreas-specific FOXA2 overexpression activated BNIP3-mediated mitophagy and conferred protection against inflammatory injury. Together, these findings uncovered a previously unrecognized mechanism whereby the FOXA2-BNIP3-AIM2 axis mitigated pancreatic and systemic inflammatory injury in ANP by enhancing mitophagy to restrain mtDNA-dependent AIM2 inflammasome activation, highlighting the FOXA2-BNIP3-AIM2 axis as a promising target for gene therapy. title: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Salmonella Typhi spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse: a case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Spondylodiscitis is an uncommon spinal infection that remains diagnostically challenging because of its non-specific symptoms and radiological overlap with tuberculosis and neoplasms. Among these, infections caused by Salmonella Typhi are extremely unusual, and the case becomes even more challenging when multidrug resistance (MDR) is present. Presentation of case We describe a 49-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension who presented with persistent back pain following an episode of enteric fever. Imaging showed spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse, initially suspected as tuberculosis or metastasis. A mammogram and tuberculosis (TB) workup were negative. Definitive diagnosis was only achieved during surgery. Intraoperative biopsy and culture confirmed Salmonella Typhi , resistant to multiple antibiotics but sensitive to imipenem and azithromycin. Targeted therapy led to clinical improvement. Clinical discussion This case underlines the diagnostic difficulty of spinal infections, where radiology alone cannot differentiate between infection and malignancy. Surgical biopsy and culture remain essential, aligning with current Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommendations. Conclusion Multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhi spondylodiscitis is exceptionally rare. Early tissue diagnosis and tailored therapy are key to achieving favorable outcomes.

Among these, infections caused by Salmonella Typhi are extremely unusual, and the case becomes even more challenging when multidrug resistance (MDR) is present.

Presentation of case

We describe a 49-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension who presented with persistent back pain following an episode of enteric fever. Imaging showed spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse, initially suspected as tuberculosis or metastasis. A mammogram and tuberculosis (TB) workup were negative. Definitive diagnosis was only achieved during surgery. Intraoperative biopsy and culture confirmed Salmonella Typhi, resistant to multiple antibiotics but sensitive to imipenem and azithromycin. Surgical biopsy and culture remain essential, aligning with current Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommendations.

Multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhi spondylodiscitis is exceptionally rare. Early tissue diagnosis and tailored therapy are key to achieving favorable outcomes.

title: Progression-free survival prediction in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: where can we further improve?
abstract: Introduction Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is a biologically heterogeneous disease in which approximately one-third of patients experience primary refractoriness or relapse despite modern chemoimmunotherapy. Although clinical prognostic indices remain the cornerstone of risk stratification, they incompletely capture the biological complexity underlying disease progression. Accurate prediction of progression-free survival (PFS) is essential to support personalized treatment strategies. Areas covered This review summarizes advances in PFS prediction in DLBCL, including clinical prognostic models, quantitative PET imaging, molecular and transcriptomic classification, genomic classifiers, tumor microenvironment profiling, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based biomarkers, and integrated multimodal prognostic models. Relevant literature was identified through PubMed, with ClinicalTrials.gov searched for ongoing clinical trials; searches were updated through 3 October 2026. We discuss the strengths, limitations, and clinical applicability of these approaches. Expert opinion Future prognostic models will increasingly rely on integrated multimodal frameworks combining clinical, imaging, molecular, immune, and dynamic response biomarkers. Among these, ctDNA has emerged as one of the most promising tools for measurable residual disease assessment. However, improving patient outcomes will require moving beyond prognostic accuracy toward predictive biomarkers capable of guiding personalized treatment selection across an evolving therapeutic landscape. Prospective validation, assay standardization, and demonstration of clinical utility will be essential for translating these approaches into routine practice.

title: Epiploic appendagitis: a review of diagnosis and treatment.
abstract: Introduction Epiploic Appendagitis (EA) is a rare, self-limiting cause of acute abdominal pain, often mistaken for conditions such as appendicitis or diverticulitis due to overlapping clinical presentations. We highlight four distinct instances of EA, emphasizing its diagnostic and therapeutic nuances. Areas covered We describe primary EA successfully managed conservatively with non-steroidal anti‑inflammatory drugs. We also describe EA with concomitant intra‑abdominal pathology requiring surgery (i.e. appendicitis) and managed conservatively with the EA (i.e cholecystitis). We further illustrate, with intraoperative and radiological imaging, the chronic sequelae of EA, a peritoneal loose body or a calcified epiploic appendage. These different types of presentations underscore the role of computed tomography as the gold-standard imaging modality for diagnosing epiploic appendagitis, characterized by hallmark findings (inflamed fat-density structures, the hyper-attenuating ring sign). Expert opinion By delineating primary and secondary EA, we aim to increase awareness among clinicians to distinguish this condition from other acute abdominal pathologies. Early recognition of EA and its benign course can prevent unnecessary surgical interventions, optimizing patient outcomes and reducing health care costs.

title: A Belgian study assessing relapsing multiple sclerosis activity through automated magnetic resonance imaging volumetry.
abstract: Aim This study assessed to what extent ico brain ms , a commercially available artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) volumetry software, detected disease activity in patients with clinically and radiologically stable relapsing multiple sclerosis (RMS), and estimated its impact on radiologists' assessments. Patients and methods We retrospectively enrolled 111 RMS patients with two consecutive MRI scans at one year interval, without relapses, progression or radiological changes while remaining on stable therapy. MRI scans were analyzed by four radiologists acting independently, and by ico brain ms . The radiologists performed their assessments both without and with ico brain ms support and categorized patient status based on lesion and brain volume changes. Results Radiologists' detection of lesion activity non-significantly increased from 6.8% to 8.6% (McNemar p = 0.215; ordinal regression p = 0.06; sign-test p = 0.08) using ico brain ms . Detection of accelerated brain volume loss increased from 2.0% to 7.7% (all p < 0.01). Inter-reader agreement improved from 36% to 56% for lesions, and from 26% to 40% for brain loss (Kendall's W, p < 0.001). Ico brain ms detected new or significantly enlarged lesions in 16.2% and accelerated brain volume loss in 6.3% of participants. Conclusion AI-assisted MRI volumetry may support radiologists to detect subclinical disease activity in patients characterized as having stable disease.

Aim

This study assessed to what extent icobrain ms, a commercially available artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) volumetry software, detected disease activity in patients with clinically and radiologically stable relapsing multiple sclerosis (RMS), and estimated its impact on radiologists' assessments.

Patients and methods

We retrospectively enrolled 111 RMS patients with two consecutive MRI scans at one year interval, without relapses, progression or radiological changes while remaining on stable therapy. MRI scans were analyzed by four radiologists acting independently, and by icobrain ms. The radiologists performed their assessments both without and with icobrain ms support and categorized patient status based on lesion and brain volume changes.

Results

Radiologists' detection of lesion activity non-significantly increased from 6.8% to 8.6% (McNemar p = 0.215; ordinal regression p = 0.06; sign-test p = 0.08) using icobrain ms. Detection of accelerated brain volume loss increased from 2.0% to 7.7% (all p < 0.01). Inter-reader agreement improved from 36% to 56% for lesions, and from 26% to 40% for brain loss (Kendall's W, p < 0.001). Icobrain ms detected new or significantly enlarged lesions in 16.2% and accelerated brain volume loss in 6.3% of participants.

AI-assisted MRI volumetry may support radiologists to detect subclinical disease activity in patients characterized as having stable disease.

title: Effectiveness of a standardised cleaning protocol to prevent malignant cell contamination during EBUS-TBNA: Results from a European multicentre study.
abstract: Background Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) and transoesophageal ultrasound with a bronchoscope (EUS-B) are key techniques for mediastinal staging in lung cancer. The 9th TNM classification underscores the prognostic importance of accurate station-specific nodal assessment. However, the optimal sampling strategy remains uncertain, particularly regarding needle reuse between N2 stations due to the risk of cross-contamination. Methods We conducted a prospective multicentre study including patients undergoing EBUS and/or EUS-B for diagnosis or staging of lung cancer or metastatic disease. title: Instance-specific brain image registration: learning deformable fields from a single image pair without external datasets.
abstract: Objective. To eliminate the reliance on large-scale external training datasets and achieve high-precision alignment for complex brain structures by overcoming the prevalent challenges of data scarcity and domain shifts in current deep learning-based registration methods. Approach. We propose a novel Instance-Specific Deep Brain Registration Framework that independently trains a dedicated model for each specific image pair. By reconceptualizing a single image pair as an internal dataset generator, we introduce a Multi-Scale Random Patch Learning strategy to construct a diverse local-to-global sample space. Architecturally, we design a Context-Aware Flow Predictor integrated with a Recurrent Context Transfer mechanism within a coarse-to-fine paradigm. Furthermore, a Topology-Aware Adaptive Optimization strategy is incorporated during the inference phase. By dynamically tracking the local spatial folding status, it adaptively adjusts spatial regularization to effectively suppress topological distortions while maximizing voxel-level accuracy. Main results. Extensive experiments on mono-modal, multi-modal, and pathological brain MRI datasets demonstrate that our method can handle large anatomical deformations without relying on external training datasets. It achieves highly competitive registration performance compared to mainstream population-based and implicit neural representation methods. Crucially, it balances this alignment precision with effective numerical topology preservation. Significance. This framework challenges the traditional population-based learning paradigm, offering a highly flexible, robust, and promising solution for practical neuroimage analysis, particularly in clinical scenarios characterized by extreme data scarcity and complex cross-modality variations.

title: Bidirectional multi-scale implicit neural representation network for topology-aware lung 4D-CT registration.
abstract: Objective. Precise lung 4D-CT registration is extremely challenging due to large respiratory excursions. To capture such large-magnitude motion, existing deep learning methods typically adopt a unidirectional coarse-to-fine cascade strategy, which is vulnerable to error propagation because uncorrected coarse-level misalignments degrade subsequent finer-scale stages and often lead to spatially inconsistent deformations. While implicit neural representations (INRs) support continuous coordinate-based deformation modeling, traditional instance-specific INRs lack clinical efficiency and struggle to converge on global large deformations because of the absence of multi-scale semantic guidance. This study aims to bridge these gaps by developing a bidirectional multi-scale INR network that jointly handles large deformation modeling and localized structural fidelity. Approach. We propose a bidirectional multi-scale INR network. First, a generalized conditional INR framework is introduced to enable continuous deformation modeling without the need for retraining. Crucially, a bidirectional feature feedback mechanism built upon Swin Transformer injects high-level semantic priors into low-resolution streams, correcting coarse-level biases through top-down interaction. Furthermore, an anatomy-aware structural constraint is incorporated to promote anatomical consistency and local boundary alignment. Main results. Under the within-subject phase-held-out DIR-Lab protocol, the proposed method achieved a mean TRE of 1.28 mm and a folding rate of 0.0090%. A leave-one-case-out evaluation assessed subject-independent generalization, yielding a mean TRE of 1.53 mm and a folding rate of 0.0195%. On the independent POPI dataset, the method achieved a mean TRE of 1.84 mm and a folding rate of 0.0806%, demonstrating competitive cross-center performance. Inference took 0.33 s per case. Significance. The proposed framework effectively combines continuous coordinate modeling with deep learning efficiency, overcoming error propagation inherent in discrete coarse-to-fine strategies and preserving both global deformation consistency and local anatomical precision. Its sub-second inference and performance under leave-one-case-out and independent external testing support its potential for efficient image-guided radiation therapy workflows.

title: EFM-GAN: enhanced feature modeling for multimodal MRI synthesis under missing-modality settings.
abstract: Objective . Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) synthesis has been widely investigated for recovering unavailable imaging modalities under incomplete acquisition scenarios. However, existing approaches often rely on implicit feature fusion strategies, where modality-specific appearance information and cross-modal anatomical representations are entangled in a shared latent space. Such entanglement may lead to unstable feature interaction and limit the preservation of modality-invariant structural information. Moreover, although multimodal MRI sequences are generally spatially registered, modality-specific acquisition mechanisms introduce heterogeneous feature distributions, leading to feature-level semantic inconsistency during cross-modal representation learning. Lesion-related details are also frequently underrepresented, particularly in anatomically complex regions that are difficult to reconstruct. Approach . To address these limitations, an enhanced feature modeling generative adversarial network (EFM-GAN) is proposed with an explicit parallel feature modeling framework. In EFM-GAN, parallel feature branches explicitly model modality-specific appearance and cross-modal shared representations. A bidirectional progressive alignment module is further introduced to progressively reduce feature-level semantic discrepancies between modality-specific representations before feature fusion, while preserving modality-dependent appearance information. Furthermore, a reconstruction difficulty-aware loss is designed to adaptively reweight reconstruction constraints, assigning greater emphasis to regions that are harder to reconstruct. Main results . Extensive experiments on the BRaTS2020 and BRaTS2021 datasets demonstrate that EFM-GAN achieves higher peak signal-to-noise ratio and structural similarity index than the evaluated baseline methods across multiple target modalities, with improved structural consistency and synthesis fidelity. Significance . The results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly modeling modality-specific and shared representations, progressively aligning heterogeneous features, and emphasizing reconstruction-difficult regions for missing-modality MRI synthesis.
