title: Volumetric chest CT report generation via state-space visual prompting and clinical-fact alignment.
abstract: Objective. To address the memory bottlenecks of three-dimensional (3D) sequence modeling and the factual hallucinations associated with cross-entropy optimization in automated 3D chest computed tomography (CT) report generation. Approach. We propose an end-to-end framework that couples perception refinement with clinical-fact alignment. First, a hybrid perception module integrates spatial visual encoding with a bidirectional state-space model to capture global anatomical topology at linear computational complexity. Second, a lesion-aware visual prompting module extracts key pathological signals through cross-view synergy and adaptive residual gating. Finally, the text decoder is fine-tuned with the group relative policy optimization algorithm under an asymmetric composite reward, reducing its reliance on normal templates. Main results. Experiments on the CTRG-Chest-548K dataset show that the proposed method achieves competitive natural language generation performance and, more importantly, a substantial improvement in clinical accuracy. The RadGraph1 score increases from 41.89 to 44.63 relative to the strongest baseline, indicating reduced factual hallucination. Significance. Combined with a 71% reduction in peak inference memory, these results indicate that the framework is a practical step toward deployable and clinically reliable automated CT interpretation.

title: 3D ultrasound shear wave elastography quantifies myocardial stiffness and anisotropy in the human heart.
abstract: Myocardial stiffness (MS) is a key property of diastolic cardiac function which is altered in various cardiomyopathies. Its quantitative evaluation remains challenging due to the myocardium's complex anisotropic fibers architecture and dynamic contraction. We developed a novel 3D shear wave elastography (3D-SWE) system suitable for clinical translation based on 3D ultrafast volumetric imaging for the quantitative assessment of MS in the human heart. Validation was performed on calibrated phantoms and ex vivo in porcine hearts compared to standard 2D-SWE. In vivo feasibility was demonstrated on healthy volunteers and patients with transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (CA). We demonstrated that 3D shear wave propagation can be observed in vivo and that 3D-SWE provides quantitative assessment of myocardium anisotropy through shear wave velocities along and across fibers and fractional anisotropy. In addition, MS was significantly elevated in CA patients compared to normal myocardium, whereas the fractional anisotropy was decreased. The feasibility of volumetric MS mapping on the human heart was demonstrated showing the potential of 3D-SWE as a clinically oriented tool for early diagnosis of cardiomyopathies such as CA.

title: 3D non-rigid motion correction using Doppler-regularized optical flow for coronary ultrasound localization microscopy in beating heart.
abstract: Objectives . Coronary microvascular disease, involving vessels smaller than 300 µ m, contributes significantly to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. However, direct visualization of coronary microcirculation remains challenging because current clinical imaging modalities lack the spatial and temporal resolution required to resolve the microvascular network. Ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) enables imaging beyond the diffraction limit and can reveal coronary microvascular structures but is altered by large motion. This work addresses 3D non-rigid motion in coronary ULM to enable more accurate reconstruction and visualization of the coronary microvascular network. Approach . Here we developed a 3D non-rigid motion correction framework based on optical flow with Doppler velocity regularization to compensate for cardiac motion in 3D ULM of beating rat hearts. Main results . The method was validated in perfused ex vivo beating rat hearts imaged with ultrafast 3D ultrasound. Motion correction enhanced microbubbles tracking density and vessels delineation, enabling visualization of microvessels below 100 µ m and velocity measurements with spatial resolution of at least 40 µ m. Significance . This framework advances volumetric assessment of coronary microcirculation, facilitating longer acquisition windows and may support future cardiovascular research and clinical applications by overcoming motion-induced limitations in 3D coronary ULM.

title: Motion-guided semi-supervised learning with dynamic kernels for cardiac cine segmentation.
abstract: Objective Accurate segmentation of full cardiac cine magnetic resonance (CMR) sequences is crucial for clinical diagnosis. Although deep learning models have become the standard for this task, they typically require exhaustive frame-by-frame supervision, making manual data annotation prohibitively time-consuming. Approach To address this, we propose a novel motion-guided semi-supervised spatiotemporal framework that propagates sparse supervision from the label of the end-diastolic (ED) frame to the entire sequence. Our framework jointly optimizes motion estimation and segmentation. First, a motion decoder estimates dense displacement fields to warp the ED label, generating high-fidelity pseudo-labels for unannotated frames. Concurrently, the segmentation network employs a Temporal Kernel Segmentation (TKS) module with dynamic convolutions to adaptively capture rapid cardiac deformations, alongside a Multi-Scale Spatial Propagator (MSP) to recover fine anatomical boundaries. The motion-derived pseudo-labels directly supervise the segmentation network, ensuring temporal coherence. Main results Extensive experiments on a multi-center cohort from three clinical centers demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms the compared methods, achieving superior segmentation accuracy and robust generalization capabilities. Significance The proposed framework effectively mitigates the burden of manual data annotation while providing temporally coherent full-cycle cardiac analysis, holding significant potential for efficient and reliable clinical assessment of cardiovascular diseases.

Objective

Accurate segmentation of full cardiac cine magnetic resonance (CMR) sequences is crucial for clinical diagnosis. Although deep learning models have become the standard for this task, they typically require exhaustive frame-by-frame supervision, making manual data annotation prohibitively time-consuming.

Approach

To address this, we propose a novel motion-guided semi-supervised spatiotemporal framework that propagates sparse supervision from the label of the end-diastolic (ED) frame to the entire sequence. Our framework jointly optimizes motion estimation and segmentation. First, a motion decoder estimates dense displacement fields to warp the ED label, generating high-fidelity pseudo-labels for unannotated frames. Concurrently, the segmentation network employs a Temporal Kernel Segmentation (TKS) module with dynamic convolutions to adaptively capture rapid cardiac deformations, alongside a Multi-Scale Spatial Propagator (MSP) to recover fine anatomical boundaries. The motion-derived pseudo-labels directly supervise the segmentation network, ensuring temporal coherence.

Main results

Extensive experiments on a multi-center cohort from three clinical centers demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms the compared methods, achieving superior segmentation accuracy and robust generalization capabilities.

Significance

The proposed framework effectively mitigates the burden of manual data annotation while providing temporally coherent full-cycle cardiac analysis, holding significant potential for efficient and reliable clinical assessment of cardiovascular diseases.

title: Segmentation-perturbation propagation in pretrained foundation-model embeddings versus IBSI-aligned radiomics for radiologist-assessed lung-nodule malignancy classification on the LIDC-IDRI cohort.
abstract: Objective Pretrained foundation-model (FM) embeddings are proposed as robust alternatives to handcrafted radiomic features, yet whether they better withstand segmentation-mask variability, the perturbation that radiomics intraclass-correlation (ICC) filtering exists to address, has not been tested head-to-head. We quantified how segmentation-mask perturbation propagates into feature reproducibility and downstream malignancy discrimination for FM embeddings and Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomics measured on a common cohort. Approach. Two 2D FM encoders (BiomedCLIP; RadImageNet ResNet50) were compared against IBSI-compliant radiomics (3D, 107 features; 2D, 102 features) on the full eligible Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) cohort: 556 lung nodules (300 malignant, 256 benign from radiologist consensus ratings, not pathology) from 399 patients. Up to thirteen perturbed masks per nodule (up to four reader masks, eight synthetic, one Dice-calibrated) were generated, and ICC(2,1) was computed across the ten perturbation conditions available for every nodule. Malignancy classification used L2-regularized logistic regression with patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Main results. Radiomics outperformed both foundation models on discrimination (AUC 0.940 and 0.930 for radiomics-2D/3D versus 0.833 BiomedCLIP and 0.798 RadImageNet; all radiomics-versus-FM differences significant by DeLong test, p≤10^(-7)). On perturbation stability the foundation models diverged: BiomedCLIP was statistically indistinguishable from radiomics (93.8% versus 90.2-92.5% stable features) and the most stable paradigm, whereas RadImageNet was significantly less stable (75.0%). A pre-specified diameter-stratified analysis showed the radiomics advantage narrows, and partly reverses, within size-matched strata; decision-curve analysis favoured radiomics. Significance. Two-dimensional foundation-model embeddings offered no discrimination advantage over IBSI radiomics under segmentation perturbation, and greater stability did not translate into greater accuracy. Perturbation stability is therefore decoupled from task-informativeness, and comparative benchmarks should report patient-grouped, size-stratified, calibration-aware metrics, not aggregate accuracy alone.&#xD.

title: Quantifying multi-lesion detection and localization in whole-body FDG PET/CT with a multimodal foundation model.
abstract: Objective . To develop a three-dimensional AI framework for detecting and localizing multiple lesions in whole-body FDG PET/CT, and to evaluate whether a pretrained PET/CT multimodal foundation model can improve lesion detection performance compared with conventional training from scratch. Approach . The AutoPET cohort comprised 1014 studies divided into 700 training, 114 validation, and 200 subject-independent test studies. Lesion masks were converted into three-dimensional bounding boxes. We developed a one-stage 3D lesion detector using a PlainConvUNet backbone to extract multi-scale encoder-decoder features for lesion classification and box regression. To leverage foundation-model representations, the PlainConvUNet backbone was initialized with weights from our previously developed multi-center PET/CT multimodal foundation model, pretrained using masked autoencoding, and subsequently fine-tuned for lesion detection. Four configurations were compared: PET+CT trained from scratch, PET only, CT only, and PET+CT initialized from the pretrained PET/CT foundation model. Detection performance was evaluated using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) and alternative FROC (AFROC) analyses, sensitivity at fixed false-positive (FP) rates, qualitative analysis, and lesion-size-stratified operating curves. Main results . Multimodal PET+CT consistently outperformed either modality alone across task-based detection metrics, demonstrating the complementary contributions of metabolic and anatomical information. Importantly, initialization from the pretrained PET/CT multimodal foundation model further enhanced lesion detection performance compared with training the same PET+CT detector from scratch, increasing absolute FROC sensitivity by 0.034-0.041 across the evaluated 1-4 FP-per-scan operating range and improving AFROC AUC by 0.028. Detection performance increased with lesion size, with small lesions remaining the most challenging. The separation between the pretrained and randomly initialized PET+CT configurations was more evident in the smaller-lesion strata, whereas their operating curves increasingly overlapped for larger lesions. Significance . This study provides a detection-centered, task-based characterization of multi-lesion analysis in whole-body PET/CT. Multimodal PET+CT improves lesion detection compared with either modality alone, lesion size is a major determinant of detection performance, and initialization from a pretrained PET/CT multimodal foundation model provides an additional performance improvement without modifying the downstream detector architecture.

title: Experimental Validation of Skull Acoustic Modelling Strategies for Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Simulation: A Cross-Comparison Study.
abstract: Objective Accurate acoustic modelling of the skull is important for simulation-guided transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) applications. However, existing skull parameterization strategies vary widely in complexity and reported accuracy. This study systematically evaluates commonly used modelling approaches to determine their predictive performance across multiple frequencies and skull types. Approach Five skull modelling strategies were assessed: two voxel-wise linear mapping models, one with fixed attenuation coefficient and one with Hounsfield unit (HU)-dependent attenuation coefficients; two three-layer models with fixed and skull-density ratio (SDR) dependent attenuation coefficient; and one single-layer fixed-parameter model. Nineteen regions of interest from five historical and two Thiel-embalmed human skulls were examined at 220 kHz, 680 kHz and 1000 kHz, bowl-surface source fields were reconstructed using holography, and intracranial pressure distributions were captured with a needle hydrophone. Measurements were compared with k-Wave simulations. Results Average simulated peak pressure errors (ɛp) ranged from 20% to 31% across frequencies, whereas intensity errors (ɛI) reached 41% to 81%. Errors in -6 dB focal volume ranged from 18% to 65%, and focal position discrepancies were typically several millimeters. Simulation generally predicted smaller insertion losses than measured, indicating a tendency to underestimate skull-related attenuation and overestimate transmitted intracranial exposure. Among the five modelling strategies, the model with the lowest observed error varied with frequency and outcome. Paired specimen-level comparisons did not establish a consistent accuracy advantage for any strategy. Significance These results indicate that current skull modelling strategies may reproduce the gross intracranial beam pattern while still misestimating the delivered acoustic exposure, focal coverage and localization. Such errors are directly relevant to tFUS dose selection, target coverage and safety-margin interpretation, underscoring the need for refined parameterization methods for reliable tFUS treatment planning.&#xD.

title: Artificial intelligence for cerebrovascular digital subtraction angiography: methods, evidence, and challenges.
abstract: Cerebrovascular diseases remain a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) provides high-spatiotemporal-resolution visualization of cerebrovascular anatomy and contrast-agent dynamics and plays an important role in diagnosis, interventional treatment planning, and treatment assessment. Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied to cerebrovascular DSA, yet the available evidence is distributed across diverse imaging settings, technical tasks, datasets, and validation strategies. This structured topical review provides a DSA-centered overview of AI-assisted cerebrovascular image analysis across 2D DSA, three-dimensional rotational angiography, and four-dimensional DSA. Literature from Web of Science Core Collection and major engineering databases was screened at title, abstract, and full-text levels using predefined eligibility criteria. The literature is organized around six interconnected tasks: image preprocessing, vessel and lesion segmentation, image registration, reconstruction and generation, disease diagnosis and detection, and hemodynamic analysis. Representative conventional and learning-based methods are reviewed together with their datasets, evaluation metrics, validation designs, and available data or code resources, with particular attention to the strength and limitations of the supporting evidence. Recent studies demonstrate increasing use of spatiotemporal modeling, deep learning, and image-generation techniques, but clinical translation remains constrained by small or single-center datasets, heterogeneous acquisition protocols and evaluation practices, limited external and prospective validation, model interpretability, and deployment requirements. Future work should emphasize acquisition-aware and physics-informed modeling, multicenter and privacy-preserving collaboration, clinically meaningful validation, and closer integration with neurointerventional workflows. By linking methodological developments with their supporting evidence and translational challenges, this review aims to support the development of more robust and clinically applicable AI methods for cerebrovascular DSA.

title: SPARC: sectorized partial-angle reconstruction based motion correction method for multi-phase CCTA.
abstract: Objective. Multi-phase coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) provides a clear visualization of coronary arteries, offering comprehensive and reliable imaging support for the clinical diagnosis of coronary artery disease. However, traditional motion correction reconstruction algorithms lack reconstruction robustness despite their interpretability, while deep learning reconstruction methods achieve high imaging quality at the expense of interpretability and anatomical reliability in clinical CCTA practice. This study aims to simultaneously achieve interpretable and robust multi-phase coronary reconstruction. Approach. We propose a motion trajectory estimation and motion correction framework termed sectorized partial-angle reconstruction-based motion correction (SPARC) for CCTA. The proposed framework integrates sectorized partial-angle reconstructions, a spatio-temporal cascaded network for coronary centerline extraction, and a phase-accumulated fuzzy C-means clustering algorithm for motion trajectory estimation. These components work together to minimize motion estimation errors and enhance the quality of motion-corrected reconstruction. Main results . Experimental results from both simulations and clinical studies demonstrate that SPARC achieves superior reconstruction performance compared with existing methods. SPARC effectively reduces coronary motion artifacts and restores clear vessel structures while preserving reconstruction fidelity, achieving the best scores on all metrics. Significance. By preserving both interpretability and anatomical reliability while effectively reducing motion artifacts, SPARC provides a clinically deployable solution for motion-corrected multi-phase CCTA, supporting more reliable imaging for coronary artery disease diagnosis.

title: Sampling-free Monte Carlo dropout approximation for single-pass uncertainty quantification in deep learning-based PET reconstructions.
abstract: Objective . Medical image reconstructions using deep learning (DL) can rapidly generate high-quality images from degraded measurements, but their clinical adoption remains challenging, largely due to the lack of fast and reliable methods to quantify aleatoric (data-driven) and epistemic (model-driven) uncertainties on a per-prediction basis. We aim to develop a computationally efficient approach for estimating both uncertainties at the voxel level in DL-based image reconstruction within a single inference run. Approach . We present a moment propagation-based framework that analytically approximates the conventional, multi-realization Monte Carlo (MC) dropout by propagating feature-map means and marginal variances through network layers, followed by a pre-calibrated correction table to compensate for covariance effects omitted in the approximation. This enables joint estimation of reconstruction, aleatoric uncertainty and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. The proposed framework was implemented on top of FastPET-a network model synthesizing PET reconstructions from time-of-flight histo-images-and evaluated in a patient pilot study of 26 total-body PET/CT acquisitions (16F-FDG and 10F-PSMA cases). Main results . Proposed method achieved relatively strong agreement with the 50-pass MC approach, with absolute differences0.5% for reconstruction,4.2% for aleatoric uncertainty and9.8% for epistemic uncertainty, along with narrow spreads across patients and tracer types, while reducing computation time by40-fold. In a complementary proof-of-concept low-count experiment, regional tracer uptake confidence intervals (CIs, derived from propagated uncertainties) widened with increased noise level, and reference uptakes consistently fell within and close to CI boundaries, indicating the proposed method could provide roughly calibrated uncertainty magnitudes reflecting quantitative prediction errors. Significance . The proposed approach provides a sampling-free and relatively accurate approximation to the multi-pass MC-based uncertainty estimation in the histo-image-based DL PET reconstruction framework. Per-prediction uncertainty quantification enables direct assessment of AI confidence and potentially supports more reliable and informed decision-making.

title: Closed-form, engine-portable uncertainty prediction of deformable image registration for dose accumulation in adaptive radiotherapy.
abstract: Objective Voxel-level uncertainty estimates of the deformation vector field (DVF) produced by commercial deformable image registration (DIR) engines are flagged as an open issue by AAPM TG-132 but seldom available, preventing principled propagation into accumulated dose-volume histograms (DVHs). We propose and validate an engine-portable per-voxel σ predictor for the DVF (μ) of a deterministic DIR, calibrated by one scalar f against landmark Target Registration Error (TRE), with no access to the engine's internals. Approach. The framework combines (i) an anisotropic Gaussian correlation kernel, longer along the cranio-caudal axis, generalising the isotropic kernel of Smolders et al. (2023); and (ii) a heuristic-residual σ_h=f[wR̃+(1-w)d̃] (default w=0.7), where R̃ combines a self-similarity descriptor residual with an image-gradient suppression factor and d̃ is |Jacobian determinant-1|, both normalised to [0,1]; σ_h is closed-form, computed from the image pair and the DVF without optimisation or training. For each combination of dataset and DIR engine (a cell), f is calibrated against TRE via grid search minimising the Landmark Expected Calibration Error (LECE). Main results. Across 4 publicly annotated computed tomography datasets (Lung-, Abdominal- and Liver-DIR-QA and DIR-LAB Castillo; 44,778 landmarks) and 4 DIR engines (ANTs SyNRA, ConvexAdam, uniGradICON, Elastix), with f fitted on other patients (5-fold cross-validation), the calibrated σ_h achieves, in the per-direction convention of Smolders et al., LECE within or below their 0.41-1.34mm range in all 16 cells (cases with final root-mean-square TRE ≤10mm retained). A constant σ calibrated likewise also meets this range, but the variation of σ_h raises the held-out log-likelihood in 13 cells; σ_h ranks landmarks by error only weakly (Spearman ρ=-0.11 to +0.34). Significance. A one-scalar, post-hoc calibration yields voxel-level DVF uncertainty for any deterministic DIR that exports its DVF, partly addressing the AAPM TG-132 gap; propagation into accumulated DVH bands is illustrated on one lung stereotactic body radiotherapy case.

title: Magnetic resonance thermometry-based estimation of equivalent radiation dose and tumour control probability in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia: a proof-of-concept and uncertainty study.
abstract: Objective To estimate the equivalent radiation dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD2Gy) and tumour control probability (TCP) from probe based and magnetic resonance (MR) temperature measurements. In addition, we evaluate how uncertainties in MR thermometry affect these metrics in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC). Approach: Temperature data were collected from three patients with LACC treated with radiotherapy and MR guided deep hyperthermia (MRgHT). Intraluminal vaginal probes provided temperature measurements at surrogate locations, while MR thermometry enabled voxel-wise temperature mapping within the target volume. These data were used to estimate EQD2Gy and TCP for combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia treatments. To assess the robustness of MR-based estimates, systematic and random temperature errors were introduced into MR thermometry data using Gaussian error models to simulate artefacts. The resulting impact on temperature distributions, EQD2Gy and TCP was evaluated using standard deviation analysis and dose volume histograms. Main results: Probe-based temperatures ranged from 39.1-39.7 °C, resulting in EQD2Gy and TCP enhancements of 2.4-4.3 Gy and 20-57 %, respectively. MR-based temperatures were higher (39.4-40.3 °C), yielding EQD2Gy (3.4-7.1 Gy) and TCP (22-68 %). Systematic temperature errors produced changes of up to 2 Gy in EQD2Gy and 5 % in TCP. In contrast, random errors - more representative of typical MR thermometry artefacts - led to minimal deviations, with changes of approximately 0.2 Gy in EQD2Gy. Within clinically relevant temperature ranges, overall uncertainties remained limited to 0.7 Gy for EQD2Gy and 1 % for TCP. Significance: MR thermometry enables voxel-based estimation of biological treatment enhancement in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia. Despite inherent temperature uncertainties, MR-based EQD2Gy and TCP estimates remain robust within clinical accuracy limits, supporting their use for treatment evaluation and future hyperthermia-informed treatment planning.

title: Capturing reader-specific annotation biases in ordinal classification: a controlled simulation study.
abstract: Objective. Inter-reader variability remains a major challenge in medical image classification, particularly for tasks involving ordinal labels, due to subjective interpretation and institutional biases. While deep learning is widely used to automate and standardize such classification tasks, including breast density assessment, handling reader-dependent annotation behavior remains an open problem. This study introduces a controlled setting to assess the extent to which such variability can be captured by a reader-adaptive model. Approach. This work builds on ReaderAdaptNet, a recently proposed reader-adaptive framework that models individual annotation styles through jointly learned reader-specific embeddings. Through a simulation study, it aims to deepen the understanding of this framework and to address the evaluation limitations imposed by small expert-annotated datasets, for which the underlying bias mechanisms are neither known nor controllable. Synthetic reader profiles are generated to reproduce realistic annotation behaviors, enabling a controlled analysis of the model's ability to adapt to diverse annotation biases. The effects of the embedding dimension and of the fusion strategy of image-reader features on classification accuracy are assessed. The structure of the embedding space is also analyzed. Main results. Results show that reader embeddings effectively capture identifiable, systematic biases, with moderate embedding dimensionality being sufficient. Systematic threshold shifts are recovered, whereas stochastic variability is not learnable. Conditioning image-reader fusion through feature-wise linear modulation or cross-attention mechanisms enables the correction of view-related discrepancies. The learned embedding space further reveals meaningful clustering of annotation profiles, reflecting similarity in reader behavior. Significance. Overall, the proposed synthetic framework identifies which aspects of inter-reader variability are learnable by ReaderAdaptNet and provides a controlled proxy for anticipating model behavior in clinical settings.

title: Enhanced diffusion model with 3D structural and segmentation priors for lung cancer radiotherapy dose prediction.
abstract: Objective Diffusion models show strong potential for high-fidelity radiotherapy dose prediction, but their performance depends heavily on the conditioning mechanism. This study introduces a novel conditioning strategy that improves volumetric consistency in slice-wise dose generation while reducing reliance on manually annotated organ-at-risk (OAR) masks. Approach We propose a diffusion-based dose prediction framework conditioned on features from the full 3D computed tomography (CT) volume and a pre-trained medical image segmentation model. A 3D feature extractor encodes global anatomical information from the entire CT volume to preserve spatial coherence across 2D dose predictions. Rather than relying on manual OAR masks, the model uses anatomical representations from the pre-trained segmentation network, integrated via cross-attention to enable anatomy-aware dose prediction. Main results The framework, Diff-Seg3D, was evaluated on three lung cancer radiotherapy datasets representing Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT), Fixed Gantry Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (FGIMRT), and 3D Conformal Radiation Therapy (3DCRT) planning techniques. It achieved the numerically lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on all three datasets, with values of 3.16, 4.38, and 4.02 Gy, respectively, and the best dose-volume histogram (DVH) scores (2.64 and 3.82) on VMAT and FGIMRT, while remaining competitive on 3DCRT. Pre-trained 3D anatomical and segmentation encoders improved the baseline diffusion model, with segmentation features improving performance without requiring explicit OAR contours at inference. Significance This conditioning strategy improves volumetric consistency and anatomical awareness in diffusion-based dose prediction. The framework can serve as a tool for generating treatment-specific, anatomy-conditioned dose priors to guide radiotherapy planning.

title: NOZOMI: a GPU-accelerated Monte-Carlo numerical approach for microstructure diffusion imaging.
abstract: Objective To develop an open-source computational framework for generating realistic white matter substrates and performing Monte-Carlo diffusion MRI simulations that use periodic boundary conditions to avoid artificial restrictions at substrate boundaries. Approach: A) A novel substrate generation algorithm was developed that ensures microstructure continuity across boundaries by adding reciprocal and replicated axons for boundary-crossing axons during substrate generation. B) A dedicated GPU-accelerated Monte-Carlo diffusion simulation engine was included, with multi-threaded CUDA implementation and simulation domain segmentation for computational efficiency. C) Validation and calibration experiments were done to verify geometric continuity across periodic boundaries, confirm simulation accuracy and precision against analytical solutions across diffusion times, compare against established simulators (Camino, Disimpy, MC/DC) under finite-pulse protocols, and guide simulation configuration. D) Diffusion time dependent axial and radial diffusivities across substrates with varying mean axon diameters and orientation dispersions were evaluated to demonstrate the utility of the framework. Main results: The framework successfully constructed complex biomimetic white matter substrates achieving high packing densities with controlled diameter distributions, orientation dispersions, beading morphology, and myelination. Monte-Carlo simulations reveal that, in both intra- and extra-axonal spaces, axon diameter primarily influences time-dependent radial diffusion, while fiber orientation dispersion primarily impacts axial diffusion. Significance: The developed framework is the first 3D white matter simulation framework to implement periodic boundary conditions for Monte-Carlo simulations without geometric discontinuity, providing approximately four times faster substrate generation than comparable tools, while facilitating controlled investigations of compartment-specific diffusion time dependence of microstructure-diffusion relationships.

title: Test-retest repeatability of MBSS-T1: a model-based, subject-specific self-supervised motion correction method for robust cardiac T1 mapping.
abstract: Objective Reliable myocardial T1 mapping is essential for quantitative cardiac tissue characterization but remains sensitive to respiratory motion, particularly during free-breathing acquisitions. This study evaluated the test-retest repeatability of MBSS-T1, a subject-specific, model-based, self-supervised deep-learning method for motion-robust myocardial T1 mapping. Approach. Seventeen healthy male volunteers aged 20-36 years underwent 3 T cardiac MRI using a 5(3)3 MOLLI acquisition under breath-hold (BH) and free-breathing (FB) conditions. Same-day repeat scans were acquired after a 20 min interval that included removal from and repositioning in the scanner. T1 maps were reconstructed using (1) MBSS-T1, (2) the contrast-agnostic deep-learning registration method SynthMorph, (3) scanner-inline motion correction, and (4) no motion correction. Repeatability was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), relative Bland-Altman analysis, within-subject coefficients of variation (CVw), relative 95% repeatability coefficients (RC95), and variance-based bootstrap inference with Holm correction. Main results. All four methods included 17 complete participant-level test-retest pairs under each breathing condition. Under BH conditions, the global ICC point estimates were 0.77, 0.64, 0.65, and 0.60 for MBSS-T1, SynthMorph, scanner-inline correction, and no correction, respectively. Under FB conditions, the corresponding values were 0.41, 0.32, 0.27, and 0.16. MBSS-T1 also had the lowest descriptive CVw under both conditions. However, none of the paired comparisons of absolute test-retest differences was significant after Holm correction (all adjusted p ≥ 0.623). The smallest Holm-adjusted variance-ratio result was obtained for MBSS-T1 versus no correction under FB conditions (variance ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.30-0.68; adjusted p = 0.058), which did not meet the prespecified significance threshold. Significance. MBSS-T1 yielded favourable descriptive repeatability estimates, particularly under FB conditions, but no pairwise comparison remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. These results characterize same-day, same-scanner measurement precision rather than absolute T1 accuracy and require confirmation in larger and more clinically diverse cohorts.

title: In silico feasibility and robustness evaluation of a single-spot proton Bragg peak FLASH platform for small-animal irradiation using a generalized 3D-printed bolus.
abstract: Objective FLASH radiotherapy has shown potential to reduce normal tissue toxicity while maintaining tumour control, motivating the development of clinical delivery strategies. However, most preclinical proton FLASH studies rely on transmission beams or spread out Bragg peaks, which do not reflect conformal clinical dose distributions. This work aims to develop and evaluate an irradiation setup for ultra-high dose-rate Bragg peak proton delivery to orthotopic mammary tumours in mice, employable in image-guided research rooms powered by clinical cyclotrons. Approach We built a simulation framework (Python+TOPAS) to assess a single spot, ablative configuration comprising a copper degrader, collimator, and generalised (3D-printed) bolus. Performance was investigated on a Phantom Mice Cohort (N=6) using personalised boluses and a Real Mice Cohort (N=10; µCT/PET) using a cohort-derived generalised bolus. Planning goals were D99%,GTV=19.0Gy and HIGTV≤1.30. Physical dose-rate feasibility was evaluated against a nominal 40Gy/s DRmin,skin threshold under an assumed 500nA beam current cap; this metric does not establish a biological FLASH effect. Robustness evaluation included 0.35 and 0.5mm setup errors and ±3% range uncertainties. Main results Simulated plans met target and heterogeneity goals across cohorts, with the 40Gy/s DRmin,skin criterion met under the assumed beam current conditions (Dmean,skin≈18.5-19.3Gy). The modelled dose-rate criterion was met below the 500nA beam current limit in both cohorts. Under the evaluated 0.35mm setup and ±3% range uncertainties, reduction in D99%,GTV remained within 3% for 9/10 real mouse cases. The generalised bolus achieved the simulated dosimetric performance across ten anatomically distinct mice; applicability to independent cohorts remains unestablished. Significance This in silico evaluation supports the simulated dosimetric and physical dose-rate feasibility of conformal Bragg peak proton delivery in small animals using a generalised bolus. The presented framework enables further development in image-guided proton research facilities, forming a strong basis for experimental validation and commissioning toward in situ small animal studies.&#xD.

However, most preclinical proton FLASH studies rely on transmission beams or spread out Bragg peaks, which do not reflect conformal clinical dose distributions. This work aims to develop and evaluate an irradiation setup for ultra-high dose-rate Bragg peak proton delivery to orthotopic mammary tumours in mice, employable in image-guided research rooms powered by clinical cyclotrons. ApproachWe built a simulation framework (Python+TOPAS) to assess a single spot, ablative configuration comprising a copper degrader, collimator, and generalised (3D-printed) bolus. Performance was investigated on a Phantom Mice Cohort (N=6) using personalised boluses and a Real Mice Cohort (N=10; µCT/PET) using a cohort-derived generalised bolus. Planning goals were D99%,GTV=19.0Gy and HIGTV≤1.30. Physical dose-rate feasibility was evaluated against a nominal 40Gy/s DRmin,skin threshold under an assumed 500nA beam current cap; this metric does not establish a biological FLASH effect. Robustness evaluation included 0.35 and 0.5mm setup errors and ±3% range uncertainties.Main resultsSimulated plans met target and heterogeneity goals across cohorts, with the 40Gy/s DRmin,skin criterion met under the assumed beam current conditions (Dmean,skin≈18.5-19.3Gy). The presented framework enables further development in image-guided proton research facilities, forming a strong basis for experimental validation and commissioning toward in situ small animal studies.&#xD.

title: Noninvasive pulse wave velocity measurement: technological progress, clinical validation, and translation challenges.
abstract: Pulse wave velocity (PWV) is increasingly recognized as a vital noninvasive metric for assessing arterial stiffness and an established independent predictor of cardiovascular risk. Despite its well-recognized clinical value, the accurate and reliable measurement of PWV remains methodologically challenging due to inherent physical ambiguities, technological heterogeneity across devices, and a lack of comparability between measurements obtained by different systems. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the physical foundations, mainstream detection technologies, signal-processing pipelines, and current clinical standardization status for PWV assessment. Although classical frameworks such as the Moens-Korteweg and Bramwell-Hill equations theoretically link PWV to the mechanical properties of the arterial wall, the intrinsic dependence of PWV on instantaneous blood pressure complicates the precise evaluation of structural arterial stiffness in clinical settings. We categorize existing measurement modalities into four principal types: mechanical-pressure sensing, optical techniques, advanced medical imaging, and emerging contactless approaches, each demonstrating unique trade-offs among measurement fidelity, clinical applicability, and operational convenience. Presently, three major barriers hinder the clinical translation of novel technologies: insufficient operational automation, inadequate cross-population validation, and a scarcity of longitudinal prognostic evidence. Future transformative advancements will likely rely on AI-driven, fully automated continuous monitoring systems optimized for real-world daily settings, large-scale multicenter trials across diverse demographics, and extensive long-term cohort studies utilizing wearable devices. These developments will collectively extend PWV assessment from intermittent clinical evaluation toward decentralized, personalized cardiovascular risk management.

title: Semi-Supervised Retinal Vessel Segmentation via SAM-Based Teacher-Student Distillation with Topology-Aware Loss.
abstract: Objective Accurate retinal vessel segmentation is critical for early diagnosis and monitoring of ocular and systemic diseases. However, deep learning methods are often limited by scarce pixel-level annotations and the inability of standard loss functions to preserve vascular topology, leading to fragmented vessel predictions. Approach We propose SAM-KD a semi-supervised framework that adapts the Segment Anything Model (SAM) for retinal vessel segmentation through a two-stage teacher-student distillation strategy. A LoRA-adapted SAM ViT-B teacher and a lightweight TinyViT-5M student are first trained on limited labeled data. The frozen teacher then generates soft pseudo-labels for unlabeled images, guiding the student through feature-level and logit-level distillation. To improve structural continuity, we introduce a graph-based connectivity loss (L conn ) that penalizes topological discrepancies based on Betti numbers and skeleton length. Main results Experiments on three public benchmarks (STARE, CHASEDB1, and HRF) using only 20% labeled data show that SAM-KD outperforms other baselines across both pixel-level metrics (Dice, sensitivity, MCC) and topological metrics (clDice, ∆b 0 , ∆b 1 ). On HRF, the proposed connectivity loss reduces ∆b 1 by 46% compared with the strongest semi-supervised baseline (38.2 vs. 71.5). The distilled TinyViT-5M student (5.4 M parameters) achieves inference in 12 ms per image with 4.9 GB VRAM, providing a 5.8× speedup and 2.9× lower memory usage than the teacher, with only a 1.1-point Dice reduction. Conclusion SAM-KD provides an effective and annotation-efficient solution for retinal vessel segmentation by combining foundation model adaptation, hierarchical distillation, and topology-aware supervision. Its lightweight design makes it suitable for real-time clinical deployment in resource-constrained environments.

title: Multivariate Searchlight Decoding of Structural Disconnection and Network Features for Predicting Post-Stroke Deficits.
abstract: Objective Lesion-symptom mapping and structural disconnection analyses have advanced our understanding of post-stroke deficits but remain predominantly based on forward inference, limiting identification of regions specifically predictive of behavioral impairment. We developed a multivariate voxelwise searchlight decoding framework for inverse inference integrating probabilistic structural disconnection with network-topological features. Approach. The analysis included 326 stroke patients from the GRECogVASC cohort assessed six months after stroke. For each patient, an age-specific probabilistic structural disconnection map was reconstructed using normative diffusion MRI tractography from 403 healthy controls. Within each voxel-centered searchlight, four features were extracted: disconnection probability, degree, clustering coefficient, and closeness centrality. Support vector machine classifiers were trained within deficit-specific decoding spaces using balanced bootstrap aggregation and majority voting to predict motor, executive, and processing-action-speed impairments. Statistical significance was assessed using 1,000 permutations, retaining voxels that consistently performed above chance across bootstrap iterations. Decoding-derived regions were subsequently assessed for within-cohort individual-level classification. Main results. Initial validation focused on left and right motor impairments, identifying predictive regions primarily within the contralateral precentral gyrus, internal capsule, and corticospinal tract, with mean accuracy ranges of 68.7-77.9%, 66.4-74.6%, and 64.8-71.8%, respectively. At the individual level, decoding-derived masks preserved overall classification performance, with accuracy improvements of up to 2.6% for individual deficits while reducing voxel dimensionality by up to 95.4%. Executive dysfunction and processing-action-speed deficits showed statistically above-chance but lower accuracies (54.5-66.9%). Executive dysfunction involved predominantly left-lateralized frontotemporal regions, whereas processing-action-speed deficits involved distributed fronto-insular, temporal, parietal, visual-association, and commissural pathways. Significance. The multivariate searchlight decoding framework integrating structural disconnection and network topology provides an inverse-inference approach complementary to lesion- and disconnection-symptom mapping for identifying spatially specific predictive patterns after stroke. The strong motor findings provide proof-of-concept support for the approach, whereas the cognitive results support its extension to distributed behavioral domains while underscoring the need for independent replication before neuroanatomical or clinical interpretation (Clinical trial registration: NCT01339195).

title: FASA-Net: a frequency-domain-enhanced and anatomically constrained vision-language framework for automated chest x-ray report generation.
abstract: Automated radiology report generation can reduce radiologists' workloads by producing preliminary reports from medical images. However, generating chest x-ray reports remains challenging. Subtle lesions and organ boundaries may be underrepresented, visual regions may be poorly aligned with medical terminology, and long reports require coherent clinical descriptions. To address these challenges, we propose FASA-Net, a vision-language framework that combines frequency-domain enhancement with anatomical semantic constraints. Its frequency-domain pyramid attention network (FPAN) integrates frequency-domain analysis and a multiscale feature pyramid to enhance local structures and high-frequency visual details. The anatomical semantic constraint attention (ASCA) module guides cross-modal interactions between visual regions and anatomy-related terms to reduce the risk of regional misalignment and semantic hallucination. The context aggregation module (CAM) incorporates a summary of the text generated so far into decoding to improve coherence and terminological consistency. Experiments on the public IU x-ray and MIMIC-CXR datasets show competitive performance on natural language generation metrics, including BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE-L, together with improved clinical label consistency measured using CheXbert-based clinical efficacy metrics. Ablation studies, visualizations, and case studies further illustrate the contributions of FPAN, ASCA, and CAM to visual detail enhancement, anatomical semantic alignment, and contextual aggregation. FASA-Net therefore has potential as an auxiliary tool for chest x-ray report generation, although clinical deployment requires further validation using multicenter data, radiologist assessments, and prospective studies.

title: DuF-DiT: Dual-Domain Fusion Diffusion Transformer with Latent Conditional Modeling for CT Metal Artifact Reduction.
abstract: Background and objective Metal implants introduce nonlinear corruptions into computed tomography (CT) projection measurements, producing severe artifacts in reconstructed images. Dual-domain metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods combine sinogram and image information to correct corrupted projections and suppress image-domain artifacts. However, their cross-domain communication commonly relies on predefined projection operations or fixed interaction pathways. In diffusion-based MAR, sustained interaction between evolving image and sinogram representations throughout the denoising process remains insufficiently explored. Methods: We introduce the Dual-Domain Fusion Diffusion Transformer (DuF-DiT), which iteratively fuses parallel image and sinogram latent representations during denoising. Its Dual-Domain Fusion Transformer blocks combine intra-domain self-attention with bidirectional cross-attention. A difference-guided gating mechanism adaptively blends conditions from metal-affected observations and linear-interpolation (LI) priors. Denoising in a CT-adaptive latent space further reduces the computational cost of the two parallel streams. Results: On synthesized DeepLesion data, DuF-DiT achieved the highest mean structural similarity index (SSIM), competitive peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and root mean square error (RMSE), and the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) in Hounsfield units (HU), with a small mean HU bias. It also achieved the lowest Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) among the compared methods. On clinical CT data, qualitative comparisons showed reduced visible artifacts with preserved anatomical structures, while DuF-DiT yielded the numerically highest mean bone-segmentation Dice coefficient on CLINIC-metal. Ablation studies supported the complementary contributions of adaptive conditioning and bidirectional cross-domain interaction. Conclusions: The results support sustained dual-domain interaction in latent space as an effective strategy for CT metal artifact reduction, with favorable image fidelity, CT-value accuracy, and downstream bone-segmentation performance under the evaluated conditions.

title: Stable training and confidence‑calibrated generation of urinary stone CT images via physics‑constrained GANs under small‑sample conditions.
abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence has become integral to modern medicine. Deep learning algorithms are widely used to assist clinical diagnosis, and medical image synthesis has become increasingly mature. However, in small-sample scenarios, synthetic images often overlook infrequent but clinically valuable lesion features. To address the challenges of training instability, insufficient authenticity, and limited clinical usability, we propose a two-stage framework based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). In the first stage, we establish a stable training and physical prior constraint framework for small-sample CT images. Specifically, we incorporate an established asymmetric normalization strategy into the WGAN-GP framework to balance generator convergence and the discriminator's Lipschitz constraint, and we embed a physical noise simulation layer at the discriminator's front end, combined with partial volume effect gradient regularization, to enhance the realism of synthesized images. In the second stage, we employ MC Dropout and deep ensemble methods to quantify uncertainty, generating uncertainty heatmaps and physically consistent confidence maps based on the Poisson-Gaussian noise model. This assists physicians in locating abnormal areas and reducing misdiagnosis risks. Through joint optimization of the generation framework, uncertainty quantification, and confidence image output, the proposed framework effectively resolves issues of mode collapse, low confidence, and poor clinical usability under small-sample conditions. The proposed framework achieves a competitive FID of 128.0, an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.072, and a high-risk recall rate of 88% for stone boundary regions, demonstrating its potential for clinically reliable synthetic CT generation.

title: Mitigating over-smoothing in Mamba via high-frequency-guided feature optimization for medical image segmentation.
abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in medical image segmentation owing to their efficient global context modeling capabilities. However, the sequential scanning mechanism of SSMs tends to induce feature over-smoothing, attenuating high-frequency lesion details and blurring irregular boundaries. In this paper, we propose HFG-Mamba, a Vision Mamba network architecture driven by high-frequency-guided feature optimization. With marginal computational and parameter overhead, the proposed architecture achieves a synergy between high-frequency prior extraction and boundary-semantic interaction. Specifically, a high-frequency prior guidance branch built upon the Discrete Wavelet Transform provides the backbone with high-frequency spatial priors. The spatial recalibration fusion block leverages these priors to counteract over-smoothing by recalibrating backbone features. The decoder further incorporates a boundary-semantic interaction module to restore boundary details degraded during upsampling. Moreover, a structure-preserving deep supervision strategy is introduced to address the optimization difficulties arising from gradient vanishing and boundary sparsity. Experiments on the ISIC17, ISIC18, and Kvasir-SEG datasets indicate that HFG-Mamba exhibits competitive performance, effectively delineating irregular boundaries and suppressing background artifacts.

title: CMRCUNet: a cross-modal calibration U-Net for acute ischaemic stroke lesion segmentation from multi-sequence MRI.
abstract: Purpose: Acute ischaemic stroke is a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, and rapid delineation of infarct lesions on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is important for supporting time-sensitive treatment decisions. Multi-sequence MRI, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), provides complementary information for characterising acute ischaemic lesions. However, many deep learning approaches process these modalities using shared encoders and direct skip connections, which may limit modality-specific feature learning and remain challenged by the severe foreground-background imbalance characteristic of stroke lesion segmentation. Method: We propose CMRCUNet, a multimodal segmentation framework that combines modality-specific residual encoders, a cross modal calibration (CMC) module, and an attention-gated decoder. The modality-specific encoders independently learn sequence-dependent representations from DWI, ADC, and FLAIR, while the CMC module performs adaptive, input-dependent weighting of modality-specific features at multiple resolution levels before decoder fusion. Focal Tversky Loss is used to address severe lesion-background imbalance. The framework is evaluated in both 2D and 2.5D configurations; the 2.5D configuration incorporates neighbouring axial slices to provide limited through-plane contextual information while retaining two-dimensional convolutional operations. Test-time augmentation (TTA) is additionally evaluated to improve inference robustness. Results: CMRCUNet was evaluated on the Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation 2022 dataset using a patient-level evaluation protocol with an independent 37-patient test cohort. The 2.5D configuration combined with TTA achieved a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.792 ± 0.142, sensitivity of 0.854 ± 0.132, specificity of 0.996 ± 0.012, and a 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 8.21 ± 8.70 mm. Conclusion: CMRCUNet provides a multimodal framework that integrates modality-specific feature extraction, adaptive CMC, attention-gated decoding, and limited inter-slice contextual information for acute ischaemic stroke lesion segmentation. The results support further investigation of adaptive CMC, particularly through external multi-centre validation.

title: Development and validation of a methodology to simulate interobserver variability.
abstract: Objective Contouring for radiotherapy planning remains time intensive. As such, interobserver contour variation (IOV) studies are limited in patient and/or observer numbers (1). This study provides a methodology to simulate IOV on images containing a single contour. Approach. 14 gynaecological cancer radiotherapy target volumes delineated by five observers on T2W-MRI scans were used to develop an AI-based approach and three rule-based (simple, normal, adapted) approaches to generate estimated minimum and maximum (min/max) contours. The rule-based approaches used delineation uncertainty of the observers' contours. The AI-based approach combined seven nnU-Net models into an ensemble. The development of the AI-based and rule-based approaches utilised 7-fold and leave-one-out cross validation, respectively. Validation used a separate/second dataset with the same characteristics and six observers. A single contour was used as the basis and the remaining five contours were used to generate the min/max contours Performance of each approach was assessed using dice similarity coefficient (DSC), mean surface distance (MSD), surface DSC (sDSC) and Hausdorff distance (HD). The best approach was utilised in a pipeline to generate a min/max contour. Multiple contours were generated between these by applying non-uniform expansions and contractions to a single contour. The comparison metrics of the observers' and simulated contours were computed in pairwise, with a mean and standard deviation calculated. Main Results. The adapted rule-based approach performed best across all metrics and was used in the subsequent pipeline. The AI-based approach had comparative median values to the rule-based approaches, but a much wider range of values. The observers' and simulated contours had a DSC of 0.77±0.13 and 0.78±0.20, respectively and an MSD of 2.4±1.7 mm and 2.2±1.5 mm, respectively. Significance. This study provides a methodology to generate additional observer contours from a single observer contour based on IOV data.

title: Arbitrary-Scale Super-Resolution for Non-Contrast Coronary MRA via Wavelet-Laplacian Enhanced Implicit Network.
abstract: Non-contrast coronary magnetic resonance angiography (NC-CMRA) provides a radiation-free and contrast-free approach for coronary assessment, but its diagnostic value is limited by insufficient spatial resolution. We propose an arbitrary-scale super-resolution framework that integrates a physiology-aware degradation model with a Wavelet-Laplacian Enhanced Implicit Network (WLEI-Net). The degradation model sequentially represents heart-rate-variability-driven asymmetric cardiac motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck respiratory translation, cardiopulmonary coupling, band-limited k-space noise, and Rician magnitude formation, and is designed to better represent the coupled physiological and k-space effects of clinical acquisitions. WLEI-Net combines SwinIR feature extraction, directional wavelet subband enhancement with channel attention, noise-adaptive Laplacian edge compensation, and a hybrid Charbonnier-wavelet-Sobel loss. Using 380 NC-CMRA images from 12 patients with a fixed patient-level split, the arbitrary-scale models were trained at 4.0× and evaluated at 2.0×, 2.5×, 3.0×, 3.5×, and 4.0×, with the four other evaluated scales unseen during training. WLEI-Net achieved the best mean performance for all six metrics at all five scales, and all comparisons against the four baselines remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction (BH-adjusted p ≤ 0.012). In a blinded two-reader evaluation of 57 test images at 2.5× and 4.0×, WLEI-Net achieved the highest mean score for artifact/noise suppression, vascular edge integrity, and small-branch visibility, with ICC(2,2)=0.817-0.901. These results support internal reconstruction and reader-perceived image-quality benefits.

title: Structural MRI Morphometry Across the Alzheimer's Disease Spectrum: Classification and Generalization.
abstract: Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides quantitative measures of brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD), but reliable classification also depends on the evaluation protocol and performance across cohorts. This study assessed a morphometry-based approach for distinguishing cognitively normal (CN) participants, those with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and those with AD. The primary cohort included 815 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), with one screening MRI per participant and predefined training, validation, and test sets. MRI records were linked to FreeSurfer measurements using exact participant and image identifiers. A multinomial L2-regularized logistic regression classifier used 42 predefined structural features and five-fold cross-validation grouped by acquisition site. In the held-out three-class test (n = 121), balanced accuracy was 0.6119 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.5291-0.6873) and the macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) was 0.7525. Recall was 0.8529 for CN, 0.2931 for MCI, and 0.6897 for AD. Additional development analyses examined demographic and clinical variables separately from the primary MRI-only result. For the binary transfer experiment, a separate ADNI-trained CN-versus-AD model using 32 shared morphometric features achieved balanced accuracy of 0.8458 and ROC-AUC of 0.9016 in site-grouped out-of-fold evaluation. The fixed model was then tested without target-cohort tuning on 181 older participants from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-1), grouped by Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR = 0 versus CDR > 0). External balanced accuracy was 0.6492 (95% CI: 0.5799-0.7158) and ROC-AUC was 0.7502. Because ADNI diagnoses and OASIS-1 CDR groups are not identical clinical endpoints, the external experiment was interpreted separately from the primary three-class analysis. The results demonstrate the value of reporting class-specific performance and independent-cohort evaluation when assessing structural MRI morphometry.

title: A conditional diffusion synthesis of DWI and ADC maps for early stroke support.
abstract: Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of disability and mortality worldwide. Effective treatment is associated with fast and effective lesion quantification from image observations. NCCT is the common first imaging to discard other neurological conditions, but it has limited sensitivity for detecting early ischemic changes. In addition, DW-MRI studies are considered the gold standard for early lesion characterization through DWI sequences and ADC maps. Nonetheless, the analysis from MRI images is delayed, restricted for some patient conditions, and typically limited because of accessibility constraints. Although recent approaches have addressed these limitations by synthesizing DW-MRI from NCCT, they often fail to reproduce ischemic lesions. Moreover, their performance is usually reported with whole-image metrics, which can overestimate image quality. This work explores the capability of conditional diffusion models to synthesize DWI sequences and ADC maps from NCCT to support care protocols in early stroke scenarios. In particular, we explore both a direct synthesis from NCCT to ADC and a conditional cascade configuration. In the cascade, the NCCT is used as a conditioning input to generate synthetic DWI findings. Then, the corresponding ADC maps are generated from the synthetic DWI. The conditional diffusion models outperformed the U-Net, Pix2Pix and CycleGAN baselines in the brain region, reaching an SSIM of 0.53 for DWI and up to 0.36 for ADC. Direct diffusion achieved a higher global ADC fidelity than cascade diffusion (SSIM 0.87 vs. 0.83), whereas cascade diffusion obtained a lower ADC error within the lesion (MAE 0.19 vs. 0.22).

title: A Supervoxel Graph-Transformer Framework for Lightweight and Interpretable Brain Tumor Segmentation from Multimodal Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of brain tumor sub-regions from multimodal MRI is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning, but most deep learning methods process millions of voxels, which is computationally demanding. We propose TransformerGNN, a supervoxel graph-Transformer framework that reformulates volumetric segmentation as node classification on a sparse graph. Each multimodal volume (FLAIR, T1, T1ce, T2) is partitioned into approximately 2,000 SLIC supervoxels, reducing about 8.9 million voxels to a region adjacency graph whose nodes carry multimodal intensity and spatial features. Stacked TransformerConv layers combine graph connectivity with multi-head attention. On BraTS 2020, the model reaches a mean Dice of 0.9002 (WT 0.9579, TC 0.8393, ET 0.9033), and 0.893 } 0.005 across repeated runs. Paired ablation tests confirm the contribution of graph connectivity and, for whole-tumor and enhancing-tumor Dice, of attention. The model has 1.36 M parameters; its network forward pass takes 0.10 s on a 16 GB laptop and uses about 1.5 GB of memory, although end-to-end processing (about 32 s per volume) is dominated by supervoxel generation. Post-hoc gradient-based saliency provides regional, modality-level attributions whose clinical value remains to be validated.

title: Geometric Motion of Multiple Liver Targets in Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy: Analysis of Translational and Rotational Motion with Different Motion-Management and Isocenter techniques.
abstract: Background Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for multiple liver targets is challenged by respiratory motion and target positioning. This study compares interfraction and intrafraction translational and rotational motion across motion management strategies (MMS) and isocentre techniques in routine clinical practice. Materials and methods: A retrospective analysis included 103 patients with 2-11 liver targets treated with abdominal compression (AC), deep inspiration breath-hold (DIBH), or free breathing (FB). Pre- and mid-treatment Cone Beam CT (CBCT) images were registered to planning CT using liver-contour matching. Translational (Anteroposterior-AP, Craniocaudal-CC, Mediolateral-ML) and rotational (pitch, roll, yaw) shifts were analysed. Motion characteristics were compared across MMS and between single-isocenter (SIC) and multiple-isocenter (MIC) approaches. Results: A total of 1102 CBCT datasets (AC: 450; DIBH: 326; FB: 326) were analysed. Shifts in CC were consistently the largest translational component across MMS. AP motion was comparable between AC and DIBH but significantly lower in FB. DIBH showed higher pitch and roll deviations. MIC exhibited higher motion than SIC, with significance in AP (AC, FB) and yaw (FB), while DIBH showed no significant differences. Intrafraction and interfraction analyses indicated greater dispersion in CC and increased variability in DIBH and FB compared to AC. A strong positive correlation between roll and inter-target distance was observed in FB, with no significant associations in AC or DIBH. Conclusion: In multi-target liver SBRT, residual translational (≤5 mm) and rotational (≤2°) deviations persist despite CBCT verification. MMS and isocenter strategy influence motion, underscoring the need for careful technique selection and individualized margins.&#xD.

title: An interpretable physics-informed graph neural network for forecasting longitudinal tau progression in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Forecasting the progression of tau pathology by modeling its spatiotemporal dynamics is critical for characterizing Alzheimer's disease (AD), where tau is a key driver of disease progression. Tau is an important prognostic biomarker for AD and is a primary endpoint for many ongoing clinical therapeutic trials. Tau burden can be quantified in vivo using positron emission tomography (PET), while its propagation is hypothesized to follow the structural connectome derived from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), providing a framework for modeling network-driven tau spread. Deep learning approaches, particularly graph neural networks (GNNs), enable data-driven learning of regional changes in tau burden by leveraging brain connectivity. However, purely data-driven models are prone to overfitting and may fail to capture biologically meaningful propagation patterns. To address this, we present here a physics-informed GNN framework for tau forecasting that incorporates prior models of tau propagation, specifically the Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov (FKPP) equation and the epidemic spreading model (ESM), as regularization terms in the latent space of the network. Our analysis relies on PET and DTI data from N=462 amyloid-positive human subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Our results demonstrate that physics-informed models improve model performance over the unregularized baseline across multiple evaluation metrics, with regularization in the latent space improving robustness compared to that in the feature space. The FKPP formulation achieves the best mean predictive performance, followed closely by ESM. We further implement post-hoc interpretability using Integrated Gradients to identify key regions and connections driving the model's predictions. The interpretability analysis is consistent with the observed performance gains, indicating that physics-based regularization yields more localized attribution within biologically relevant regions. Overall, our findings demonstrate that integrating prior formulations of tau propagation with GNNs enhances predictive accuracy and interpretability, providing a promising framework for modeling network-driven spread of tau pathology.

title: Optimizing Rib Remodeling: A Data-Driven Model for Personalized Waist Contouring.
abstract: Background Rib cage remodeling procedures, like rib osteotomy with osteosynthesis, have shown promise for waist narrowing in aesthetic surgery. However, the ideal osteotomy location and bending angle remain poorly defined. Objectives This preclinical, proof-of-concept study aimed to: (1) quantify how osteotomy location and rib bending angle affect rib apex displacement using a large, computed tomography (CT) dataset, and (2) develop a data-driven framework as a first step toward guiding selection of rib number, osteotomy site, and bending angle tailored to individual waist contour goals. Methods Using the open-source RibFrac CT dataset, 600 ribs (300 eleventh [XI] and 300 tenth [X]) were segmented with the RibSeg deep learning tool. Displacement at the rib apex was computed using a chord-perpendicular method. title: A multi-reader multi-case study comparing Breast Cancer Reading Efficiency and Accuracy in Screening with Tomosynthesis versus AI-assisted mammography.
abstract: Objectives Full-field digital mammography (FFDM) is the standard for breast cancer screening but has reduced sensitivity in dense breasts. Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) improves cancer detection compared to 2D mammography but is limited by cost and longer reading times. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced mammography has demonstrated improved sensitivity compared to 2D mammography. This study compares AI-enhanced 2D mammography (DM+AI) with DBT in recalling interval breast cancers (IBCs). Methods : A multi-reader, multi-case crossover study was conducted using the Emory BrEast Imaging Dataset, which includes paired FFDM and DBT images with biopsy-proven outcomes. Six radiologists reviewed 53 IBC and 53 screen-detected cancer (SDC) cases, with random assignment to DM+AI or DBT, followed by crossover after a washout period. Primary outcomes included recall rate of IBCs. Secondary outcomes included recall rate of SDCs, interpretation time, and subgroup analysis by breast density. Results : For IBCs, DM+AI and DBT demonstrated similar recall rates (41.5% vs 40.9%) and detection rates (14.8% vs 11.9%). DM+AI identified more non-invasive (31.5% vs 13.0%) and mass-forming (61.0% vs 21.8%) cancers. For SDCs, recall and detection rates were comparable across modalities. In fatty breasts, recall was higher with DM+AI (91.7% vs 50.0%), while DBT performed better in extremely dense breasts. DM+AI enabled faster interpretation, averaging 24.1 seconds less per case. Conclusion : AI-enhanced 2D mammography demonstrated comparable performance to DBT with shorter interpretation times, supporting a stratified screening approach. Advances in knowledge This study is the first direct comparison of AI-enhanced mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis for IBC detection.

title: Quantitative Hepatobiliary MRI for Early Prognostic Assessment After Liver Transplantation: Survival Prediction Using the Contrast Enhancement Index.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the feasibility and prognostic value of the contrast enhancement index (CEI) derived from gadobenate dimeglumine (Gd-BOPTA)-enhanced hepatobiliary-phase (HBP) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for early assessment of liver graft function after liver transplantation (LT). Methods This retrospective study included LT recipients undergoing Gd-BOPTA-enhanced MRI within 6 months after transplantation. CEI was calculated using liver-to-psoas signal intensity ratios on pre-contrast and HBP images acquired 90-120 minutes after contrast administration. ROC, Kaplan-Meier, and age-adjusted Cox regression analyses evaluated associations with mortality. Results Seventy patients (median age, 62 years; interquartile range [IQR], 48-74) were included. CEI was quantifiable in all cases (median, 1.27; IQR, 1.09-1.37). Non-survivors had significantly lower CEI values than survivors (median, 1.17 vs 1.31; p = 0.03; Cliff's δ = -0.28). ROC analysis showed moderate discrimination for mortality (AUC, 0.667; 95% CI, 0.529-0.793), with an optimal cutoff of 1.301 (sensitivity, 88%; specificity, 51.2%). Patients with CEI <1.301 had significantly lower overall survival (log-rank p = 0.028). After adjustment for recipient age, CEI remained associated with mortality (HR per 0.1-unit increase, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.98; p = 0.035). Conclusion Quantitative CEI measurement on Gd-BOPTA HBP MRI is feasible after LT, and lower CEI values. Advances in knowledge This study links quantitative Gd-BOPTA-enhanced HBP MRI with overall survival after LT, supporting CEI as a potential non-invasive imaging biomarker for postoperative risk stratification.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Procedural Efficiency of ACR TI-RADS, EU-TIRADS, and K-TIRADS in ≤ 10 mm Thyroid Nodules Using Bethesda Cytology: A Cohort of 998 Nodules.
abstract: Objectives To compare the diagnostic performance and procedural efficiency of American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (ACR TI-RADS), European Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (EU-TIRADS), and Korean Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (K-TIRADS) in ≤ 10 mm nodules using Bethesda cytology as the reference standard. Methods This retrospective study included 998 nodules ≤10 mm undergoing ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB). Primary analyses included Bethesda II (negative) and Bethesda V-VI (positive) nodules excluding Bethesda I/III/IV, yielding 604 nodules (540 negative; 64 positive). Categories 1-3 were considered low risk and 4-5 high risk under a harmonized threshold Diagnostic performance and classification patterns were compared. Results K-TIRADS showed the numerically highest sensitivity (93.8%) and negative predictive value (NPV) (97.9%), although sensitivity did not differ significantly between systems, with lower specificity (35.4%) and accuracy (41.6%).EU-TIRADS showed intermediate performans (sensitivity 68.8%, specificity 73.7%, accuracy 73.2%). ACR TI-RADS achieved the highest specificity (83.3%) and accuracy (81.0%) with lower sensitivity (60.9%). Low-risk classification rates were 78.6% (ACR), 69.2% (EU), and 32.3% (K) of nodules; false-positive high-risk classifications among Bethesda II nodules were 16.7%, 26.3%, and 64.6%, respectively. Conclusion In ≤ 10 mm nodules, the three systems demonstrated distinct diagnostic and classification profiles under a harmonized TR4-5 threshold, with different trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity. Advances in knowledge Applying a harmonized TR4-5 threshold in ≤ 10 mm nodules reveals substantially differences in classification patterns among the three systems, demonstrating that they are not interchangeable under a uniform risk threshold.

title: Construction and Validation of a Prediction Model for TACE Resistance in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Based on Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Radiomics.
abstract: Objective To construct and validate a contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) radiomics-clinical model for predicting transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods A total of 168 HCC patients who underwent CEUS on two vendor platforms (Philips E9 and GE Logiq E95) were split into a training set (n = 118) and an internal validation set (n = 50), with an additional 80 patients forming an external validation cohort. For each patient, 2D regions of interest were manually delineated on the largest cross-sectional slice of each CEUS phase. Radiomic features were extracted and screened by LASSO regression; the twelve retained features were linearly combined into a single Rad-score. The Rad-score and three prespecified clinical risk factors (tumor size, Child-Pugh class, AFP) confirmed by multivariate analysis were combined into a parsimonious logistic regression (LR) model with four predictors in total. Performance was assessed by ROC curve, calibration curve, decision curve analysis (DCA), subgroup analysis, and prospective validation. Results The combined model had AUCs of 0.895, 0.891 and 0.846 in three sets, with subgroup AUCs >0.86. Prospective validation showed TACE plus sorafenib improved 6-month response rate from 26.7% to 53.3% for high-risk patients. Conclusion The CEUS radiomics-clinical model accurately predicts TACE resistance, guiding individualized HCC treatment. Advances in knowledge This model integrates CEUS multi-phase radiomics and clinical factors, outperforming single clinical/radiomic models. Strict multi-step screening and comprehensive validation avoid data leakage, ensuring robust prediction and clinical translatability.
