title: Diagnostic value of multiparametric MRI radiomics combined with serum PSA and tissue P504S for prostate cancer.
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic value of multiparametric MRI radiomics features combined with serum PSA-related indicators and tissue P504S expression for prostate cancer, and to develop a multimodal auxiliary diagnostic model in a retrospective cohort that was not restricted to early-stage disease. Clinical, imaging, and pathological data from 126 patients with suspected prostate cancer were retrospectively collected and divided into a prostate cancer group (69 cases) and a benign lesion group (57 cases). All patients underwent prostate MRI; radiomics features were extracted, and LASSO regression, with 10-fold cross-validation for tuning, was used to construct a Rad-score. Serum t-PSA, f-PSA, f/t-PSA ratio, and PSAD were measured. Tissue P504S expression was detected by immunohistochemistry and semi-quantitatively scored. A combined diagnostic model was constructed using multivariate logistic regression. ROC metrics were evaluated in the model-development cohort and are reported as apparent performance. AUC differences between models were compared using the DeLong test. The prostate cancer group had higher t-PSA and PSAD and a lower f/t-PSA ratio than the benign lesion group (all P < .001). P504S was positive in 64/69 cancer cases (92.8%) and 9/57 benign cases (15.8%; P < .001). Eight radiomics features were selected, and the median Rad-score was 0.86 in cancer cases and - 0.52 in benign cases (P < .001). The full model combining Rad-score, f/t-PSA, PSAD, and tissue P504S semiquantitative score achieved an apparent AUC of 0.956 (95% CI: 0.918-0.994), sensitivity of 92.8%, specificity of 91.2%, PPV of 92.8%, and NPV of 91.2%. The overall imaging + serum model had an apparent AUC of 0.912 (95% CI: 0.856-0.968). In exploratory location-based analyses, AUCs were 0.962 for peripheral zone lesions and 0.934 for transition zone lesions. The full model showed promising apparent discrimination for prostate cancer in this retrospective cohort and may represent a potential auxiliary diagnostic model after tissue sampling. The imaging + serum model could potentially support biopsy decision-making, whereas the full model requires tissue P504S assessment and may assist diagnostic confirmation or risk characterization. Neither incremental clinical benefit nor a reduction in unnecessary biopsies has been established. Internal and external validation and evaluation of the practical clinical workflow are required before routine use.

title: Prenatal clinical features and clinical outcomes of fetuses with 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion syndrome: A single-center case series of 22 patients.
abstract: This study analyzes 22 fetuses with 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion syndrome in Eastern China to investigate the prenatal clinical features and postnatal outcomes. We conducted a retrospective study of 22 fetuses diagnosed with 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion (312-855 kilobase) via chromosomal microarray analysis among 2607 prenatal cases from January 2022 to September 2024. Parental origin, ultrasound findings, and postnatal outcomes were evaluated. The 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion prevalence was 0.84% (22/2607). Prenatal ultrasound anomalies were observed in 54.5% (12/22), primarily mild cardiac findings (tricuspid regurgitation), choroid plexus cysts, and thickened nuchal translucency. Parental testing (13 cases) revealed 6 paternal, 6 maternal, and 1 de novo case. Postnatal follow-up of 18 live births (mean 14.7 months) showed normal development in most cases (17/18), with 1 child exhibiting delayed language development. Four pregnancies (18.2%) were terminated despite genetic counseling. Our study underscores that the 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion exhibits incomplete penetrance and variable prenatal phenotypes, complicating outcome prediction. Long-term pediatric follow-up is essential, and early reassurance should be avoided even in cases with normal prenatal findings or favorable short-term outcomes.

title: Synchronous hepatocellular carcinoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma in a patient with chronic hepatitis B: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale Synchronous double primary cancers involving hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) are exceptionally rare. Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is an established cause of HCC, whereas Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is the major etiological factor for NPC. We report a patient with synchronous HCC and NPC and review the relevant literature. Patient concerns A 63-year-old Chinese man with chronic HBV presented with a liver mass detected on routine screening. He reported nasal obstruction. Diagnoses Contrast-enhanced imaging showed a 46 × 59 mm hepatic lesion with portal vein tumor thrombus and a 41 × 29 mm nasopharyngeal mass with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsies confirmed moderately differentiated HCC and EBV-associated non-keratinizing NPC. Final diagnoses were HCC Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer Stage C (CNLC IIIa, Child-Pugh A) and NPC T3N2M0 Stage III (AJCC 8th edition). Interventions He received hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC, mFOLFOX) combined with tislelizumab and donafenib; radiotherapy for NPC was deferred after shared decision-making. Entecavir was continued. Outcomes At 19-month follow-up, both tumors remained controlled; the NPC met radiographic complete response criteria. Lessons Synchronous HCC and EBV-associated NPC were controlled during treatment with a tislelizumab-containing multimodality regimen, and the NPC achieved a radiographic complete response. The contribution of each treatment component cannot be determined from a single case, and definitive radiotherapy remains the standard of care for locoregionally advanced NPC. Multidisciplinary management and close monitoring are essential.

title: Successful rechallenge with almonertinib and corticosteroids after gefitinib-induced interstitial lung disease: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale First-generation epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are highly effective in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, drug-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD) remains a rare but potentially fatal adverse event. The safety and efficacy of EGFR-TKI rechallenge - either with the same agent or an alternative one - following ILD resolution are not established and represent a significant clinical knowledge gap. Patient concerns A 53-year-old never-smoking woman with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma - detected to harbor an L858R mutation in exon 21 of the EGFR gene - developed progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia after 2 months of first-line gefitinib therapy, despite confirmed initial radiographic and clinical response. Diagnoses The patient was diagnosed with grade 3 gefitinib-associated ILD. Interventions With the discontinuation of gefitinib, the patient was given methylprednisolone to resolve ILD. To control advanced lung adenocarcinoma progression, the patient was subjected to 6 cycles of treatment using pemetrexed, carboplatin, and bevacizumab, with measurable tumor shrinkage, followed by maintenance therapy with bevacizumab. Furthermore, given the tumor progression 14 months later, the patient was prescribed docetaxel plus bevacizumab to restore control. Ten months later, the patient experienced disease progression and strongly requested to use EGFR-TKIs again given prior response to EGFR-TKI. The patient was rechallenged with almonertinib, a third-generation EGFR-TKI, and methylprednisolone. Outcomes The patient had measurable tumor shrinkage, with sustained tumor control and no recurrence of pulmonary toxicity. As of last follow-up, she maintained progression-free survival for approximately 8 months on almonertinib. Lessons This case provides a hypothesis-generating observation, illustrating feasibility only in highly‑selected patients with EGFR‑mutant NSCLC and prior severe TKI‑related ILD. With prophylactic corticosteroids and rigorous surveillance, third‑generation EGFR‑TKI may represent a tentative clinical option for such patients, but general safety cannot be inferred from this single case.

title: Risk-adapted active surveillance for prostate cancer: Can mpMRI, biomarkers, and genomic classifiers reduce biopsy burden without compromising safety?: A systematic review.
abstract: Background Active surveillance is the preferred management strategy for men with low-risk and selected favorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer. However, conventional surveillance protocols rely heavily on repeated systematic biopsies, which impose procedural morbidity, patient burden, and limited precision in identifying true disease progression. Risk-adapted tools, including multi parametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI), molecular biomarkers, and genomic classifiers, have emerged as potential strategies to optimize surveillance intensity while preserving oncologic safety. To systematically evaluate the evidence supporting risk-adapted AS strategies incorporating mpMRI, molecular biomarkers, and genomic classifiers, with a focus on reducing biopsy burden without compromising oncologic outcomes. Methods A systematic review was conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched for peer-reviewed studies evaluating mpMRI, molecular biomarkers, or genomic classifiers within AS cohorts. Randomized controlled trials and prospective or retrospective cohort studies reporting surveillance-related outcomes were included. Primary outcomes included biopsy upgrading or reclassification, AS failure, and oncologic safety endpoints. Due to methodological heterogeneity, results were synthesized narratively. Results Five publications met inclusion criteria, representing four unique studies one randomized controlled trial and three observational cohorts and 1215 participants. The 2 Active Surveillance Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study publications were treated as linked reports from the same trial. Baseline mpMRI with targeted and systematic biopsy was associated with lower subsequent AS failure and upgrading, but biopsy avoidance was not directly tested. An MRI-led cohort omitted routine protocol biopsies, although the absence of a concurrent comparator precluded conclusions about equivalent oncologic safety. The 4Kscore demonstrated potential for confirmatory-biopsy triage; a hypothetical deferral strategy could have avoided 27% of biopsies but would have missed 2 Grade Group 2 upgrades. The Decipher genomic classifier independently predicted biopsy upgrading, although biopsy reduction was not evaluated. Evidence establishing the long-term oncologic safety of biopsy reduction remained insufficient. Conclusion Risk-adapted AS strategies incorporating mpMRI, molecular biomarkers, and genomic classifiers may improve risk stratification and support selective adjustment of biopsy intensity. However, current evidence does not establish the safety of routine biopsy omission or fully biopsy-free surveillance. Integration of these tools should remain individualized, with histologic reassessment when indicated and prospective validation of biopsy-deferral strategies.

title: Lattice radiotherapy followed by chemoimmunotherapy for sustained disease control in bulky centrally located left hilar lung squamous cell carcinoma: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Bulky centrally located, locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer often abuts critical thoracic structures, making both upfront surgery and conventional radiotherapy dose escalation challenging. Lattice radiotherapy (LRT) may achieve tumor debulking while limiting radiation exposure to surrounding organs at risk. Patient concerns A 70-year-old man presented with a recurrent cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis for 6 months. Diagnoses Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography revealed a 6.6 cm × 6.0 cm irregular left hilar mass with mediastinal invasion, encasement of the adjacent trachea and vessels, and an indistinct interface with the esophagus. Bronchoscopic biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. The programmed death-ligand 1 tumor proportion score was 18%. The final diagnosis was left hilar lung squamous cell carcinoma, cT4N1M0, stage IIIA. Interventions After multidisciplinary team discussion, the patient underwent LRT followed by sequential paclitaxel, carboplatin, and tislelizumab, and then maintenance tislelizumab monotherapy. Outcomes After 3 treatment cycles, the maximum lesion diameter decreased from 6.6 cm to 4.4 cm, meeting the criteria for partial response according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1. Cough and hemoptysis resolved, and the squamous cell carcinoma antigen level decreased from 11.5 to 3.9 ng/mL. At the last follow-up, 12 months after treatment initiation, the lesion remained stable without definite disease progression, and no grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events were observed. Lessons For selected patients with bulky, centrally located, locally advanced lung squamous cell carcinoma who are potentially resectable but at high surgical risk, LRT followed by chemoimmunotherapy may be a feasible individualized strategy. The role of conversion surgery should be determined by dynamic multidisciplinary risk-benefit assessment.

title: Adrenal ganglioneuroma in an adolescent presenting as an incidentaloma: Imaging-pathology correlation and diagnostic challenges: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Adrenal ganglioneuroma (AGN) is a rare, benign, and usually nonfunctioning tumor arising from neural crest-derived sympathetic ganglion cells. Preoperative diagnosis is difficult because the clinical presentation is often nonspecific, and imaging findings overlap with those of other adrenal neoplasms. We describe an adolescent adrenal incidentaloma with detailed imaging-pathology correlation, adding to the small number of reported adolescent cases. Patient concerns A previously healthy 16-year-old male underwent contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) after a bicycle accident. No traumatic injury was identified, but imaging incidentally revealed a well-circumscribed right adrenal mass measuring approximately 6.1 cm × 3.6 cm × 5.0 cm. Diagnoses CT and magnetic resonance imaging showed progressive, persistent enhancement across the arterial, venous, and delayed phases without demonstrable washout (attenuation increased from 20 Hounsfield units unenhanced to 55 Hounsfield units in the venous phase, with further qualitative enhancement on 15-minute delayed images) and no intralesional fat, suggesting a non-adenomatous lesion and raising suspicion for a neurogenic tumor. Biochemical evaluation showed no evidence of hormonal hypersecretion. Histopathological examination after resection established the diagnosis of AGN. Interventions The patient underwent right adrenalectomy because of the size and radiologically indeterminate nature of the mass. Outcomes The postoperative course was uneventful. Transient elevation of blood pressure noted during follow-up prompted biochemical reevaluation, which showed no evidence of excess catecholamine. Follow-up CT at 9 months showed no recurrence. Lessons Progressive delayed enhancement without washout and absence of signal loss on opposed-phase magnetic resonance imaging, a pattern previously described in ganglioneuroma, may suggest the diagnosis preoperatively, although definitive diagnosis requires histopathological confirmation. Complete surgical excision established the diagnosis and achieved a favorable short-term outcome; the excellent long-term prognosis of AGN is supported by the published literature, and our patient remains recurrence-free at 9 months.

title: Metastatic G2 laryngeal neuroendocrine tumor treated with sulfatinib and sintilimab: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale Laryngeal neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are rare and heterogeneous malignancies with limited evidence guiding the management of metastatic disease. We report a metastatic G2 laryngeal NET initially presenting as an unusual temporal subcutaneous metastasis and subsequently treated with combined targeted therapy and immunotherapy. Patient concerns A 63-year-old man with a history of invasive lung adenocarcinoma presented with a 1.3 × 1.2 cm left temporal subcutaneous nodule and a history of hoarseness accompanied by throat pain. Diagnoses Histopathological examination of the temporal lesion suggested metastatic NET. Subsequent PET-CT, laryngoscopy, and biopsy identified a primary laryngeal NET. After vertical partial laryngectomy, right neck dissection, and laryngeal function reconstruction, pathology confirmed a well-differentiated G2 NET with cervical lymph-node and temporal subcutaneous metastases, classified as pT2N1M1, stage IVC. In March 2025, hepatic metastases were pathologically confirmed. Molecular profiling identified HRAS p.Q61L, KDR p.S265L, and ROS1 p.S615Y variants, microsatellite instability-high status, and programmed death-ligand 1expression with a combined positive score of 70. Interventions Combination therapy with sulfatinib (300 mg/day) and sintilimab (200 mg every 3 weeks) was initiated in April 2025 and continued without dose reduction, interruption, or delay. Outcomes After 10 months of combination therapy, contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a reduction in the size of hepatic metastatic lesions compared with baseline, together with a marked decrease in the number of metastatic lesions. The largest index hepatic lesion decreased from 32.68 mm to 19.05 mm in maximal diameter, corresponding to a 41.7% reduction, demonstrating a marked radiological reduction in hepatic metastatic burden. At the latest documented assessment in February 2026, no further disease progression or treatment-related adverse events were observed. Lessons This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of metastatic laryngeal NET with an unusual subcutaneous presentation. Comprehensive pathological and molecular evaluation may aid treatment decision-making in advanced disease. The observed disease control with sulfatinib plus sintilimab is hypothesis-generating and requires validation in additional patients.

title: Serial changes in myocardial fluorodeoxyglucose uptake on routine oncologic PET during breast cancer chemotherapy: are they clinically relevant?
abstract: Objective Cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction is an important prognostic factor in patients with breast cancer undergoing chemotherapy. We evaluated serial changes in myocardial fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake on routine oncologic PET and assessed whether these changes differed according to chemotherapy regimen. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 535 FDG PET examinations obtained before and after chemotherapy in 108 patients with breast cancer. Mean FDG uptake was measured in the myocardium with the highest accumulation and in the descending aorta on the same cross-section, and their ratio was defined as the myocardial standard uptake ratio (M-SUR). Chemotherapy regimens were classified as anthracyclines, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI), and others. Pre- and post-treatment M-SUR values were compared using the paired t-test. Results A total of 309 paired examinations were analyzed: anthracyclines, 34 pairs (n = 17); HER2 inhibitors, 146 pairs (n = 40); ICI, 20 pairs (n = 9); and others, 109 pairs (n = 54). M-SUR significantly increased after anthracycline therapy (3.45 ± 2.44 to 5.37 ± 3.67, P = 0.046) and ICI therapy (3.78 ± 2.94 to 4.98 ± 4.27, P = 0.0328). No significant change was observed in the HER2 inhibitor or other regimen groups. Conclusion Serial FDG PET demonstrated regimen-dependent increases in myocardial FDG uptake after anthracycline and ICI therapy. Routine oncologic PET may reflect chemotherapy-related myocardial metabolic alterations.

title: Prediction of pathologic complete response in breast cancer patients undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy using baseline 18F-FDG PET/CT-derived CT radiomics and clinicopathological biomarkers.
abstract: Objective The study aimed to assess whether baseline fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/computed tomography (CT)-derived CT radiomics adds predictive value to clinicopathological biomarkers and PET metabolic assessment for pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) in breast cancer. Methods This retrospective study included 104 patients with stage I-III breast cancer who underwent baseline 18F-FDG PET/CT, NAC, and surgery. Clinicopathological variables and tumor maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) were recorded; 107 CT radiomic features were extracted using PyRadiomics. Clinical, Metabolic, Radiomics, and Combined models were developed using L2-regularized logistic regression and evaluated by nested five-fold cross-validation. Discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis were assessed; 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using 1000 bootstrap resamples of pooled out-of-fold predictions. Results Forty-six patients (44.2%) achieved pCR. Area under the curves (AUCs) were 0.784 (95% CI: 0.686-0.875) for Clinical, 0.595 (0.470-0.704) for Metabolic, and 0.636 (0.526-0.739) for Radiomics models. The Combined model had the highest numerical AUC (0.797; 95% CI: 0.705-0.880), with accuracy 0.731, sensitivity 0.630, specificity 0.810, and F1-score 0.674. Conclusion Combining CT radiomics and SUVmax with clinicopathological biomarkers yielded the highest numerical discrimination for pCR, but improvement over the Clinical model was modest. Larger multicenter external validation is needed before clinical implementation.

title: Diagnostic performance of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography in primary tumor localization and its impact on management in patients with metastases of unknown origin: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: Aim Metastases of unknown origin (MUO) remain a diagnostic challenge, with identification of the primary tumor closely tied to treatment planning and survival. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) in detecting the primary tumor in MUO patients. Method This cross-sectional study included 73 patients with MUO who underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT at the Department of Clinical Oncology and Nuclear Medicine, Assiut University Hospitals, between November 2023 and December 2025. PET/CT findings were correlated with histopathological or clinical-radiological follow-up to classify results as true/false positive/negative. Result Median age was 64 years (37 males, 36 females). PET/CT suggested a primary tumor site in 76.7% (56/73) of patients. PET/CT correctly localized the primary in 50 patients (true positive), was falsely positive in 6, falsely negative in 2, and correctly excluded a detectable primary in 15 (true negative). Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and accuracy were 96.15, 71.4, 89.3, 88.2, and ~89%, respectively. Lung was the most common identified primary (20%), followed by lymphoma and ovarian cancer (10% each). PET/CT altered tumor, node, metastasis staging or diagnosis in 10 patients (13.7%): 3 (4.1%) were upstaged to M1b, 2 (2.7%) were downstaged to M0, and 5 (6.8%) were reclassified as nonmalignant based on PET/CT findings. Conclusion 18F-FDG PET/CT is a high-yield, single-step imaging tool for evaluating MUO, showing a primary tumor detection rate and diagnostic accuracy favorable relative to previously published series, and significantly influencing clinical management strategies. Given the modest sample size and heterogeneous reference standard, these findings should be regarded as preliminary pending validation in larger, multicenter cohorts.

This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) in detecting the primary tumor in MUO patients.

This cross-sectional study included 73 patients with MUO who underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT at the Department of Clinical Oncology and Nuclear Medicine, Assiut University Hospitals, between November 2023 and December 2025. PET/CT findings were correlated with histopathological or clinical-radiological follow-up to classify results as true/false positive/negative.

Result

Median age was 64 years (37 males, 36 females). PET/CT suggested a primary tumor site in 76.7% (56/73) of patients. PET/CT correctly localized the primary in 50 patients (true positive), was falsely positive in 6, falsely negative in 2, and correctly excluded a detectable primary in 15 (true negative). Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and accuracy were 96.15, 71.4, 89.3, 88.2, and ~89%, respectively. Lung was the most common identified primary (20%), followed by lymphoma and ovarian cancer (10% each). PET/CT altered tumor, node, metastasis staging or diagnosis in 10 patients (13.7%): 3 (4.1%) were upstaged to M1b, 2 (2.7%) were downstaged to M0, and 5 (6.8%) were reclassified as nonmalignant based on PET/CT findings.

Conclusion

18F-FDG PET/CT is a high-yield, single-step imaging tool for evaluating MUO, showing a primary tumor detection rate and diagnostic accuracy favorable relative to previously published series, and significantly influencing clinical management strategies. Given the modest sample size and heterogeneous reference standard, these findings should be regarded as preliminary pending validation in larger, multicenter cohorts.

title: Image-guided and augmented reality-assisted robotic surgery.
abstract: Purpose of review Image-guided and augmented-reality (AR)-assisted robotic surgery is moving from static preoperative visualization toward dynamic, automated navigation. This review summarizes evidence from the past 12-18 months on three-dimensional (3D) virtual models, AR, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted registration in robotic urology, focusing on which applications have moved to comparative and randomized evidence, and on how far this rationale now generalizes beyond the centers that first described it. Recent findings In radical prostatectomy, a randomized trial of AI-driven 3D-AR guidance vs. cognitive MRI guidance showed lower overall positive margins, less postoperative radiotherapy, and better 12-month continence. In partial nephrectomy, 3D models have progressed from anatomical planning to perfusion-mapped clamping and automated AI-based registration, with favorable outcomes across comparative, meta-analytic, and propensity-matched series, including in horseshoe kidneys and totally endophytic tumors. Independent European groups have reported automated registration, segmentation, and nephrometry tools, and small series have extended image guidance to kidney transplantation, vena cava thrombectomy, upper tract urothelial carcinoma, and testicular cancer surgery. Summary Randomized evidence in prostatectomy, a maturing pathway in partial nephrectomy, and growing independent replication support an expanding but still procedure-limited role for image-guided robotic surgery. Standardized protocols, objective accuracy metrics, multicenter validation, and structured training remain necessary before wider adoption.

title: Biomarker testing in prostate cancer.
abstract: Purpose of review Biomarker testing is increasingly incorporated into diagnostic and postdiagnostic pathways for early prostate cancer (PCa), but its optimal clinical positioning remains uncertain. We provide a clinically oriented framework for biomarker use, from risk-adapted detection and biopsy decision-making to postdiagnostic risk stratification and management selection. Recent findings Blood-based biomarkers, including PHI, 4Kscore, Stockholm3, and IsoPSA, improve risk stratification beyond PSA alone and may reduce unnecessary imaging and biopsy, although their clinical utility varies according to the diagnostic setting and their integration with MRI. Urine-based assays, including SelectMDx, MyProstateScore and MyProstateScore 2.0, and ExoDx, provide additional approaches to prebiopsy risk refinement, with newer multigene tests showing improved discrimination for clinically significant PCa. After diagnosis, tissue-based genomic classifiers such as Decipher, Oncotype DX Genomic Prostate Score, and Prolaris may refine prognostic stratification and management selection, but prospective evidence demonstrating improved outcomes from biomarker-guided treatment remains limited. Summary Biomarkers can refine risk assessment across early PCa, but clinical utility varies by assay and setting.

title: Psychosis With Cognitive Impairment in a Young Adult: Case Report.
abstract: Cognitive symptoms are an often-undervalued dimension of psychotic disorders that are overshadowed by positive symptoms that are more striking and more the target of treatment. Nevertheless, cognitive symptoms affect up to 80% of patients with primary psychotic disorders and exert a decisive impact on prognosis, quality of life, and functional outcomes. Processing speed, attention, and memory are the most consistently affected domains, with greater impairment observed in individuals with predominantly negative symptoms. Cognitive deficits often predate the onset of the first episode of psychosis, but their long-term trajectory remains the subject of debate, which oscillates between neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative models. Importantly, cognitive dysfunction in schizophrenia is broader and more persistent than in affective psychoses and shows limited improvement with antipsychotic treatment. We report the case of a 19-year-old woman with a first episode of psychosis who presented with predominantly positive symptoms along with profound cognitive impairment. Neuropsychological assessment revealed severe deficits in attention, fluency, memory, and executive functioning, with a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of 12/30 during her acute presentation. Extensive workup excluded other physical and autoimmune etiologies, although cranial MRI showed bilateral mesiotemporal atrophy, a finding consistent with cognitive dysfunction in psychotic spectrum disorders. Treatment with paliperidone led to remission of psychotic symptoms and partial cognitive improvement (Montreal Cognitive Assessment 21/30), yet substantial deficits persisted, impacting autonomy, insight, and social functioning. This case illustrates the emblematic role of cognitive impairment in psychotic disorders, highlighting its early onset, persistence despite symptomatic remission, and limited responsiveness to dopamine-targeted treatments. Emerging therapies-such as modulators of the cholinergic system, erythropoietin derivatives, and cognitive remediation strategies-represent promising avenues to address these unmet needs.

title: Utilizing Voxel-Based Specific Regional Analysis as a Noninvasive Examination of a Rare Case of Very-Late-Onset Schizophrenia-Like Psychosis.
abstract: We present a rare, atypical case of very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis (VLOSLP) in a 78-year-old male patient with a family history of schizophrenia and thought withdrawal. Although the patient showed no clinically significant cognitive impairment, we evaluated the medial temporal lobes of the brain for prodromal changes using the voxel-based specific regional analysis system for Alzheimer disease (VSRAD), a magnetic resonance imaging-based volumetric software program. The patient had gradually developed psychosis, including experiencing thought withdrawal, over almost 1 year before admission. His daughter had been diagnosed with schizophrenia at the age of 20 years. After careful examination, the patient was diagnosed with VLOSLP. We analyzed the target volume of interest for disease-specific atrophy obtained from VSRAD. The Z score for the target volume of interest was 1.42, which was too low for a diagnosis of Alzheimer disease. These results suggest that the patient's psychosis in this case might not have been due to the prodrome of Alzheimer disease. The patient responded well to treatment with a low dose of a single atypical antipsychotic. The use of noninvasive procedures such as VSRAD for the evaluation of prodrome in dementia in patients with VLOSLP is expected to become routine in the future.

title: Brief Report: Prognostic Value of Kaposi Sarcoma Herpes Virus-Associated Clinical Symptom Scores in HIV-Associated Kaposi Sarcoma.
abstract: Background Kaposi sarcoma herpes virus (KSHV)-associated inflammatory cytokine syndrome (KICS) is defined by clinical, laboratory, and radiographic findings and KSHV viremia. Whether the presenting clinical symptoms of KICS have prognostic value in patients with HIV-associated Kaposi sarcoma (HIV-KS) initiating therapy is unknown. Setting Two prospective clinical trials were conducted among participants with mild-to-moderate (A5264/AMC067) and advanced (A5263/AMC066) HIV-KS in low-income and middle-income countries. All participants received antiretroviral therapy, and chemotherapy was given according to the randomly assigned treatment arm. Methods We developed a Kaposi sarcoma clinical symptom score (KSCS score), derived from the previously described KICS definition to determine whether the score could inform prognosis. The score ranging from 0 to 3 was based on increasing severity of clinical manifestations. We evaluated the impact of baseline KSCS score on progression-free and overall survival using Cox proportional hazard regression. Results Of 190 participants in A5264/AMC067 and 329 in A5263/AMC066, 150 (78.9%) and 239 (72.6%) had KSCS score ≥1 and 15 (7.9%) and 95 (28.9%) had KSCS score 3, respectively. Independent of the treatment arm, participants with KSCS score 3 had a higher risk of death (A5264/AMC067: adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) = 9.17; 95% CI: 3.60 to 23.41; A5263/AMC066: aHR = 2.99; 95% CI: 1.69 to 5.28) and shorter progression-free survival (A5264/AMC067: aHR = 2.36 95% CI: 1.26 to 4.43; A5263/AMC066: aHR = 2.31; 95% CI: 1.23 to 3.60) compared with those with KSCS score ≤2. Conclusions KSCS score symptoms are common, especially in advanced HIV-KS. KSCS score 3 is associated with higher risk of progressive KS disease or death, despite treatment with antiretrovirals and chemotherapy. This population may benefit from improved diagnostic and management options.

title: AI-Assisted Interpretation of Prostate MRI: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) improves detection of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) but is limited by inter-reader variability. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly applied to prostate segmentation and lesion detection, with heterogeneous results. Concerns remain regarding generalizability, data set bias, and validation. This review summarizes recent evidence on AI-assisted prostate MRI interpretation, identifies knowledge gaps, and outlines directions for future research. A systematic literature search of PubMed and Google Scholar was performed for studies published between January 2023 and April 2025 evaluating AI-assisted interpretation of biparametric or multiparametric prostate MRI. Reference lists were manually reviewed. Eligible studies assessed diagnostic performance of AI alone or in combination with radiologists. Eighteen studies met inclusion criteria from 157 screened. Standalone AI systems achieved areas under the curve (AUCs) ranging from 0.77 to 0.91, with sensitivities of 65.4% to 96% and specificities of 77.6% to 91%, occasionally outperforming radiologists. Hybrid AI-radiologist models improved inter-reader agreement, reduced interpretation time by up to 50%, and enhanced detection accuracy for equivocal (PI-RADS 3) lesions. AI assistance particularly benefited junior and general radiologists, improving diagnostic performance, confidence, and reproducibility. In active surveillance cohorts, AI demonstrated greater accuracy than radiologists for detecting disease progression (AUC=0.86 vs. 0.69), although specificity limitations persisted. Overall, AI integration into prostate MRI workflows demonstrates substantial potential to improve detection efficiency and standardization. Broader clinical adoption will require large-scale, multicenter validation, harmonized imaging protocols, and rigorous outcome-based evaluation.

title: Diagnostic Feasibility and Physical Assessment of Lung CT Images Reconstructed From Ultra-Low-Dose Positioning Scan for Computer-Aided Nodule Detection.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the diagnostic feasibility of computer-aided detection (CAD) of pulmonary nodules on CT images reconstructed from volumetric ultra-low-dose (ULD) positioning scans compared with standard-dose CT. Methods In this retrospective study, 160 adults with at least 1 pulmonary nodule underwent volumetric ULD positioning scans and standard-dose CT. One target nodule per patient was analyzed. CAD sensitivity was evaluated on 5-mm volumetric ULD positioning scans and 5-mm standard-dose CT according to nodule size, morphology, and malignancy. An additional analysis was performed using 1-mm volumetric ULD positioning scans, with 1-mm standard-dose CT serving as the reference standard. Physical image characteristics were assessed using phantoms. Results A total of 160 nodules (median size: 5 mm) were analyzed. CAD sensitivity was 71.3% (114/160) for 5-mm volumetric ULD positioning scans and 85.0% (136/160) for 5-mm standard-dose CT (P<0.01), with reduced sensitivity most apparent for small nodules. With 1-mm volumetric ULD positioning scans, sensitivity improved to 88.8% (142/160). However, noninferiority to reference 1-mm standard-dose CT was not demonstrated using a 15-percentage-point margin (P=0.084). The median estimated effective dose was 0.18 mSv for volumetric ULD positioning scans and 4.67 mSv for standard-dose CT. Phantom assessment showed lower spatial resolution and increased low-frequency noise for volumetric ULD positioning scans. Conclusion Thinner-slice reconstruction improved CAD sensitivity on volumetric ULD positioning scans; however, noninferiority to standard-dose CT was not demonstrated. Further optimization of image quality and CAD performance is warranted.

title: Can CT Phantoms Produce Realistic CT Images of Human Anatomy? Physics-Based Evaluation of Multimaterial 3D-Printed CT Phantoms From CT Data.
abstract: Objectives Patient-specific computed tomography (CT) phantoms can be produced using a novel 3D-printing technique that aims at replicating measured CT image volumes with high anatomic fidelity and accurate CT values. The purpose of this study is a comprehensive physics-based evaluation of both technical phantoms and a full-size adult abdominal phantom with regard to image-quality metrics and the reproducibility of CT values. In addition, the visualization of abdominal pathologies will be assessed. Materials and methods The study was conducted in 3 steps. First, a geometric reference disc phantom (40 mm thickness, 150 mm diameter) was 3D-printed using multimaterial jetting and scanned on a commercial photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) to assess the CT values of the base materials used for printing and to evaluate the influence of the printing process on spatial resolution and noise properties. Second, CT images of the reference phantom reconstructed with a medium-sharp and a sharp kernel were used as templates to print 2 CT-derived disc phantoms using multimaterial jetting with voxel-based material mapping. These phantoms were then scanned to assess how template image sharpness propagates into the image-quality properties of the final printed phantoms. Spatial resolution was evaluated using edge spread function (ESF) analysis and edge rise distance (ERD), whereas noise characteristics were assessed using noise power spectrum (NPS) analysis. Third, as a proof of concept, a full-size adult abdominal phantom was 3D-printed with a patient CT data set as template. Phantom images were compared with patient images regarding CT values, spatial resolution, noise properties, and the depiction of pathologic structures. Results Evaluation of the CT attenuation of the base materials showed that CT values ranging from -37 HU to 995 HU in virtual monoenergetic images at 60 keV can be printed.For the reference disc, measured ESF curves showed close agreement with theoretical expectations across all reconstruction kernels, indicating preservation of spatial resolution by the printing process. CT-derived discs showed minor edge smoothing compared with the reference for smooth and medium-sharp reconstructions. For sharp reconstructions, edge smoothing was severe, with an ERD increase of up to 32% compared with the reference. Edge smoothing was more pronounced for the disc based on a sharp template. NPS were highly consistent across all discs, with only minor differences in peak amplitude. In the abdominal phantom images ESF and NPS closely matched those of the patient CT images. Measured attenuation agreed well for tissues with positive CT values up to 1000 HU. Fat was represented with increased CT values because of print material limitations. Clinically relevant pathologic structures, including a large hepatocellular carcinoma and a smaller focal liver lesion, were displayed comparably in the phantom images. Conclusions CT phantoms generated from CT image volumes using 3D printing with multimaterial mapping on a voxel level accurately reproduce the template images in terms of image sharpness, noise characteristics, and attenuation properties of tissues with positive CT values not exceeding 1000 HU. The achievable spatial resolution is limited to medium-sharp levels and does not improve by using sharper template images. These findings support the use of image-based multimaterial 3D printing to produce realistic anthropomorphic phantoms for advanced CT image-quality assessment and optimization, and for validation of reconstruction algorithms and quantitative CT imaging methods.

Phantom images were compared with patient images regarding CT values, spatial resolution, noise properties, and the depiction of pathologic structures.

Results

Evaluation of the CT attenuation of the base materials showed that CT values ranging from -37 HU to 995 HU in virtual monoenergetic images at 60 keV can be printed.For the reference disc, measured ESF curves showed close agreement with theoretical expectations across all reconstruction kernels, indicating preservation of spatial resolution by the printing process. CT-derived discs showed minor edge smoothing compared with the reference for smooth and medium-sharp reconstructions. For sharp reconstructions, edge smoothing was severe, with an ERD increase of up to 32% compared with the reference. Edge smoothing was more pronounced for the disc based on a sharp template. NPS were highly consistent across all discs, with only minor differences in peak amplitude. In the abdominal phantom images ESF and NPS closely matched those of the patient CT images. Measured attenuation agreed well for tissues with positive CT values up to 1000 HU. Fat was represented with increased CT values because of print material limitations. Clinically relevant pathologic structures, including a large hepatocellular carcinoma and a smaller focal liver lesion, were displayed comparably in the phantom images.

Conclusions

CT phantoms generated from CT image volumes using 3D printing with multimaterial mapping on a voxel level accurately reproduce the template images in terms of image sharpness, noise characteristics, and attenuation properties of tissues with positive CT values not exceeding 1000 HU. The achievable spatial resolution is limited to medium-sharp levels and does not improve by using sharper template images. These findings support the use of image-based multimaterial 3D printing to produce realistic anthropomorphic phantoms for advanced CT image-quality assessment and optimization, and for validation of reconstruction algorithms and quantitative CT imaging methods.

title: Photon-Counting CT for Postoperative Imaging of Cochlear Implants: Comparison to Flat-Detector CT.
abstract: Objectives After FDA approval in 2021, photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCCT) has demonstrated its feasibility for high-resolution imaging while lowering the radiation dose at the same time. High-resolution visualization of cochlear implant (CI) integrity and positioning is crucial for postoperative management. The aim of this study was to evaluate the performance of PCCT for postoperative imaging after CI implantation in comparison to high-resolution flat-detector CT (FDCT), the current clinical gold standard. Materials and methods Postoperative PCCT scans after cochlear implantation were retrospectively analyzed from August 2024 to April 2026. Scans were included for analysis if FDCT acquisition had been before PCCT on the same patient in the course of sequential bilateral cochlear implantation. Image quality was assessed in consensus by 2 experienced readers using a scoring system analyzing structural delineation of the inner and middle ear, CI integrity, metal and motion artifacts as well as calculating an overall score. Radiation dose was retrieved from the picture archiving and communication system. Results Twenty-eight postoperative PCCT scans of patients after CI implantation with a mean time delay of 4.5±5.1 years between FDCT and PCCT scans were evaluated. Image quality of PCCT was noninferior to FDCT for all single imaging features (P<0.001, eg, distinction of single CI electrodes: median [interquartile range] PCCT 3 [3 to 3]; FDCT 3 [3 to 3]; P<0.001) with the exception of the homogeneity of bony structures and the mastoid cell septation (P=0.999). PCCT was superior to FDCT in reducing metal and motion artifacts and increasing the delineation of the stapes (P=0.009 to <0.001; eg, metal artifacts PCCT 3 [2.75 to 3]; FDCT 2 [1 to 2]; P<0.001). Effective radiation dose of PCCT was 0.05±0.01 mSv and 8.8±5.4-times lower than for FDCT with 0.44±0.29 mSv (P<0.001) applying our institutional protocols. Conclusions Regarding image quality in postoperative assessment of CI, PCCT is noninferior to or in single features better than FDCT at a significantly lower radiation dose and shorter scan time.

title: Primary Brain Sarcoma Presented on FDG PET/CT.
abstract: A 62-year-old man had dizziness and dysarthria for 4 months and limited mobility of the left upper extremity for 1 month. An outside enhanced MR showed a space-occupying lesion in the right frontal lobe. Since the patient had pancreaticoduodenectomy, gastrostomy, and jejunostomy 8.5 years ago for poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the small intestine, brain metastasis was suspected. FDG PET/CT demonstrated increased FDG activity in the right frontal lobe lesion, but no FDG-avid lesion was found in other parts of the body. Following surgical resection, histopathology examination indicated sarcoma. The patient underwent brain radiotherapy afterward.

title: Intense Focal Renal 18F-MFBG Uptake Attributable to Radiation in a Pediatric Patient With Neuroblastoma.
abstract: A 9-year-old boy with neuroblastoma was enrolled in a clinical trial. After radiotherapy to the primary tumor site, 18F-MFBG PET/CT was performed 2 months later. No abnormal radiotracer accumulation suggestive of metastatic disease was identified. However, focal intense 18F-MFBG uptake was observed in the upper pole of the left kidney, within the previously irradiated field. No structural renal lesion was identified on cross-sectional imaging, and no evidence of renal tumor was found during 12 months of clinical and imaging follow-up. This case illustrates that intense localized renal 18F-MFBG uptake may result from radiation and should be recognized as a potential pitfall in post-radiotherapy 18F-MFBG PET/CT interpretation.

title: 18F-FAPI PET/CT and Cardiac Magnetic Resonance for Cardiac Fibrotic Process in End-stage Renal Disease: A Pilot Study.
abstract: Background End-stage renal disease (ESRD) increases the risk of myocardial fibrosis. This study aimed to detect cardiac fibroblast activation and fibrosis in ESRD using 18F-labeled fibroblast activation protein inhibitor (FAPI) PET/CT and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). Patients and methods This prospective clinical trial (NCT07107919) enrolled 33 ESRD patients who underwent 18F-FAPI PET/CT, with 19 patients undergoing CMR. Myocardial FAPI activity was quantified. Cardiac function [left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), right ventricular ejection fraction (RVEF), left atrial ejection fraction (LAEF)] and tissue parameters [native T1, extracellular volume (ECV), late gadolinium enhancement (LGE)] were assessed by CMR. Spearman correlation analysis assessed correlations between 18F-FAPI uptake and CMR parameters. Results A total of 75.76% (25/33) of ESRD patients showed myocardial FAPI uptake, significantly higher than the controls (P < 0.05). 18F-FAPI-42 PET identified more segments with evidence of fibroblast activation than CMR-late gadolinium enhancement detected fibrosis (82 vs. 71). Compared with FAPI-negative patients, FAPI-positive patients had increased native-T1, decreased LVEF, LAEF and RVEF (P < 0.05). FAPI-positive segments showed higher native-T1 and extracellular volume % than FAPI-negative segments (P < 0.05). FAPI activity correlated with LVEF, RVEF, LAEF and native-T1. Higher myocardial FAPI uptake was associated with lower LVEF and longer dialysis duration. Conclusions 18F-FAPI PET enables in vivo detection of cardiac fibroblast activation in ESRD and correlates with functional and tissue parameters by CMR. FAPI uptake may serve as an imaging biomarker for cardiac remodeling. Further studies are warranted to clarify the role of 18F-FAPI PET in evaluating the efficacy of anti-fibrotic treatment and in assisting cardiac risk stratification in ESRD patients.

title: An Anatomy-Guided Frontal Sinus Setback Workflow Using Patient-Specific Cutting Guides and Resorbable Fixation in Chinese Transfeminine Patients.
abstract: Frontal sinus anterior-table setback is a technically demanding component of forehead feminization when simple burring is insufficient to achieve the desired contour. We describe a structured operative workflow in 4 Chinese transfeminine patients aged 20 to 32 years. Preoperative computed tomography (CT) and virtual surgical planning were performed with ProPlan CMF, and a patient-specific cutting guide was used to localize the frontal sinus boundaries and the anterior-table osteotomy line. After reduction of the brow and supraorbital region, the mobilized anterior-table was repositioned posteriorly according to its relationship with the adjacent reduced bony contour and stabilized with a RapidSorb 2.0 resorbable plate-and-screw system, avoiding permanent metallic hardware in this non-load-bearing region. The frontal sinus mucosa was preserved without curettage, sinus obliteration was not performed, and the nasofrontal outflow tract was preserved. All patients underwent postoperative day-5 CT to document the early anterior-table position and frontal bony contour and completed 6 months of clinical and photographic follow-up. Improvement in forehead contour was observed without major complications. Because concomitant facial procedures were performed in selected patients, overall facial appearance reflects the combined effects of these procedures. This report presents preliminary technical experience with resorbable rigid fixation for frontal sinus anterior-table reconstruction; larger series with longer clinical and radiographic follow-up are needed to assess long-term skeletal stability, frontal sinus-related outcomes, and fixation behavior after material resorption.

title: Intracranial Aneurysm Complicated by Common Carotid Artery Infarction Following FDS Procedure.
abstract: Flow-diverter stents (FDS) are widely used in the endovascular reconstruction of large, wide-necked intracranial aneurysms; their mechanism of action primarily involves altering the hemodynamics within the aneurysm to promote thrombus formation. They represent a highly promising device for the treatment of intracranial aneurysms. When treating aneurysms located in the anterior circulation, key branches may be covered by the flow-diverter stent. The incidence of occlusion in these branches has been reported in the literature; moreover, even when branch occlusion occurs, associated neurological deficits are extremely rare. However, postoperative occlusion of the common carotid artery following flow-diverter stent placement is also extremely rare in clinical practice. This paper reports a case of a patient who developed left common carotid artery occlusion following the implantation of a fine-mesh stent. One year after the placement of a Surpass Evovle Flow Diverter System fine-mesh stent, the patient presented with symptoms such as impaired limb movement during a follow-up examination. Cranial MRI revealed a left frontoparietal cerebral infarction. Following treatment with enteric-coated aspirin tablets, the patient's symptoms improved, and they were discharged. The aim of this study is to analyze the mechanism of occurrence and the management process by combining intraoperative, postoperative imaging, and follow-up data, while reviewing the relevant literature to explore the risk factors, clinical characteristics, and prevention and treatment strategies for this complication.

title: Surgical and Cosmetic Outcomes After Fronto-Orbital Advancement With Hybrid Fixation for Unilateral Coronal Craniosynostosis: A Single-Center Cohort Study.
abstract: Background Fronto-orbital advancement (FOA) remains the standard surgical treatment for unilateral coronal craniosynostosis, particularly in patients presenting beyond the age window for endoscopic treatment and in those with significant frontal and orbital deformity. However, postoperative relapse, residual asymmetry, and fixation-related limitations remain important clinical concerns. Fixation strategies aim to provide immediate structural stability while minimizing potential interference with subsequent cranial growth. Objective To evaluate surgical, morphometric, cosmetic, and perioperative outcomes after FOA using a hybrid fixation strategy in patients with nonsyndromic unilateral coronal craniosynostosis. Methods This retrospective single-center cohort study included 14 patients treated between January 2023 and December 2024 at the JSC National Center for Neurosurgery, Astana, Kazakhstan. All patients had CT-confirmed unilateral nonsyndromic coronal craniosynostosis and underwent primary FOA with combined fixation using biodegradable plates in key structural regions and absorbable sutures between individual remodeled bone fragments. Cosmetic outcomes were assessed using the Whitaker classification and clinician-rated Visual Analog Cosmetic Score (VACS), with each patient's VACS calculated as the mean of independent ratings from 10 assessors. Morphometric evaluation combined cephalic index (CI), as a measure of overall cranial width-to-length proportions, with frontal asymmetry index (FAI), orbital assessment, and nasal deviation angle (NDA). Perioperative safety outcomes and follow-up data were also analyzed. Results The mean age at surgery was 16.7±12.9 months, and mean follow-up was 16 months (range 12-24). Favorable cosmetic outcomes were achieved in all patients: 92.9% were classified as Whitaker class I and 7.1% as class II, with no class III or IV outcomes or revision surgeries. Median postoperative VACS was 9.5 (range 6-10). FAI categories decreased in 10 of 14 patients (exact sign test, P=0.002; Holm-adjusted P=0.006). CI categories decreased in 6 patients (P=0.031; Holm-adjusted P=0.063), without establishing normalization of cranial shape. NDA categories showed no evidence of a directional change (P=0.625). All 14 patients received intraoperative autologous blood reinfusion and additional allogeneic blood transfusion. Mean total hospital stay was 18.9±3.5 days, including both preoperative and postoperative inpatient care. No major postoperative complications, cerebrospinal fluid leakage, surgical-site infection, relapse, or reoperation were observed. Conclusion Extended FOA with hybrid fixation was associated with favorable early cosmetic outcomes in this retrospective cohort. These findings describe the combined reconstructive procedure and do not establish the independent contribution of fixation, preservation of physiological cranial growth, or superiority over alternative fixation methods. Larger comparative studies with longer follow-up are required.

title: Skull Clamp-Related Frontal Sinus Fracture in a Patient With Polyostotic Fibrous Dysplasia: Complication and Management.
abstract: Three-pin skull clamps provide head fixation, but skull fracture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak are rare, reported complications. Fibrous dysplasia, which structurally weakens bone, may increase this risk. A 37-year-old man with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and previous cranioplasty underwent prone posterior fossa decompression and cranial contouring. The anterior pin caused a crush injury with an open anterior table fracture of the frontal sinus; postoperative computed tomography also revealed a minimally displaced posterior table fracture, and rhinorrhea suggested CSF leak. At next-day reoperation, a minimal dural injury was found; after mucosal removal and nasofrontal duct occlusion, the dura and posterior table fracture were sealed with fascia lata, and the sinus was obliterated with a dermofat graft. The anterior table was refixed with plates and covered with titanium mesh, and a pedicled galeopericranial flap was interposed beneath the injured skin. At 3 months, there was no hardware exposure, infection, or rhinorrhea.

title: EvoBrainNet: A Multi-Objective Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search With Self-Adaptive Mutation for Volumetric Brain Tumor Segmentation.
abstract: Accurate brain tumor segmentation in volumetric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains a significant challenge due to the heterogeneity in tumor shape, size, location, and intensity. To address this, we propose EvoBrainNet, a multi-objective evolutionary framework that optimizes both segmentation accuracy and model efficiency. We design a modular 3D search space comprising three core components: the ExoFeature module for enhanced contextual encoding, the DRAP (dilated residual attention pyramid) module for multiscale attention and channel recalibration, and the RefineUp module for decoder-side refinement via attention-guided upsampling. These modules are embedded into a supernet architecture supporting scalable and flexible architectural search. An evolutionary neural architecture search (NAS) with a self-adaptive mutation strategy enables dynamic exploration of architectures based on performance feedback. The search jointly optimizes segmentation quality, measured by dice similarity coefficient (DSC), and model efficiency, evaluated by parameter count and floating-point operations (GFLOPs). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first multi-objective evolutionary NAS framework employing self-adaptive mutation for brain tumor segmentation. Experiments on the BraTS 2021 dataset show that EvoBrainNet achieves state-of-the-art performance with a 95.74% DSC and 1.30 mm HD95, along with high IoU, precision, recall, and specificity. It outperforms twelve existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency. Moreover, it exhibits consistent performance across diverse datasets, obtaining 93.55% DSC on BraTS 2020, 94.35% DSC on MSD Brain Tumor, and 82.61% DSC on ACDC. Ablation and statistical analyses confirm the contribution of each module and the effectiveness of the adaptive mutation strategy.

These modules are embedded into a supernet architecture supporting scalable and flexible architectural search. An evolutionary neural architecture search (NAS) with a self-adaptive mutation strategy enables dynamic exploration of architectures based on performance feedback. The search jointly optimizes segmentation quality, measured by dice similarity coefficient (DSC), and model efficiency, evaluated by parameter count and floating-point operations (GFLOPs). title: VQ-CSDN: A Vector Quantized Content-Stain Decoupling Network for Stain Normalization of H&E Histopathology Images.
abstract: Stain normalization is a fundamental preprocessing technique in digital and computational pathology, and it is important for improving the consistency of clinical diagnosis by reducing color heterogeneity. However, existing stain normalization methods are often limited by content-stain entanglement and an ambiguously modeled content-stain relationship, resulting in unstable structural preservation, cross-center adaptation burden, and sensitivity to template selection. To address these limitations, we propose a Vector-Quantized Content-Stain Decoupling Network (VQ-CSDN) that decouples structure-defining content from stain appearance and learns a center-specific content-to-stain mapping, enabling structure-preserving, template-free stain transfer from unseen source centers without source-specific retraining. VQ-CSDN employs two independent encoders to extract content and stain features respectively and a generator for reconstruction. To better characterize cross-center content feature spaces and capture staining styles, we introduce vector quantization with a global content codebook shared across centers and center-specific stain codebooks. Moreover, a content-to-stain module directly infers stain features from the content feature and a target staining style, enabling end-to-end stain transfer without template selection. To further promote structural fidelity and enhance staining style separability, we propose center-specific gradient-driven discriminators that jointly assess center-level stain conformity and the morphological consistency of generated images. Extensive experiments on multiple public and private pathology datasets show that VQ-CSDN consistently enhances normalization quality, reflected by increased SSIM/PSNR and decreased FID, and further improves downstream benign-malignant classification performance (AUC 0.9738) over state-of-the-art methods.

title: Graph-Based Minimally Supervised Risk Stratification for Prognosis Prediction in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction.
abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is associated with poor outcomes, with 5-year survival after hospitalisation as low as 35-40%. Despite its growing prevalence, effective treatments remain limited. A major barrier to therapeutic success is the substantial biological and clinical heterogeneity within HFpEF, suggesting that distinct patient profiles may require different management strategies. This study investigates whether graph-based machine learning methods can identify distinct patient clusters within the HFpEF population and assess their relationships with clinical characteristics and outcomes. We analysed a multimodal dataset of 133 symptomatic HFpEF patients, comprising more than 240 K attributes derived from comprehensive cardiovascular assessment. These included cardiac MRI, echocardiography, circulating biomarkers of fibro-inflammation, and high-resolution proteomics. Five conventional unsupervised clustering methods were first applied but failed to produce clinically coherent groups, largely due to the complexity and multimodality of the data. To address this, we implemented a minimally supervised Graph Neural Network (GNN) that incorporated limited label information while modelling relationships between patients. This approach produced five clusters with potential clinical relevance. Importantly, cluster membership remained significantly associated with survival after adjustment for established clinical risk factors, including age, sex, BNP levels, symptom burden, and kidney function. Internal validation yielded an accuracy of 0.706 and an $F1$-score of 0.613, indicating reasonably consistent performance and suggesting that graph structure may aid generalisation and class-wise prognostic prediction. Overall, the findings show that minimally supervised graph-based learning can more effectively capture the underlying structure of multimodal HFpEF data than traditional methods. Visualisation and cluster quality metrics further support the effectiveness of the GNN approach.

title: TransXplainRRG: A Radiologist-Evaluated LVLM for Chest Radiograph Report Generation.
abstract: Recent advancements in Large Vision- Language Models (LVLM) enhance X-ray report generation, but often neglect clinical context, overlook workflow integration, and lack explainability, which hinders clinical adoption due to interpretability and reliability concerns. This paper addresses the dual challenges of performance and expert explainability in automated X-ray report generation for clinical AI applications. Our proposed approach, TransXplainRRG, utilises an off-the-shelf Swin Transformer model along with a transformer-based text encoder that incorporates patient medical history to generate a radiology report. Further, we explore an expert-guided 'inside-out' approach and extract only abnormal findings for radiology report refinement. Thus, this study bridges the gap between high-performance automation and interpretability critical for clinical practice by combining state-of-the-art transformer-based vision encoders, text encoders, and LLMs. TransXplainRRG is trained and tested on the large-scale MIMIC-CXR dataset and further evaluated on the unseen IU X-Ray dataset to demonstrate its generalizability and robustness. We employed the GREEN metric as a complementary measure of clinical consistency, achieving scores of 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray, both higher than those achieved by MAIRA-2 under the same evaluation setting. It also performed competitively across standard evaluation metrics, frequently matching or surpassing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we introduce qualitative evaluation metrics developed from radiologists' viewpoints and conduct a preliminary radiologist evaluation on 100 generated reports to assess their clinical relevance. Quantitative and qualitative analyses further demonstrate the potential of our TransXplainRRG framework for reliable and explainable radiology report generation.

title: DualSeg: Unified Multi-Scale Framework With Dual-Stage Encoder For Glomerular Segmentation.
abstract: Glomerular segmentation in whole-slide histopathology is essential for quantitative renal assessment, yet it is fundamentally challenged by local texture discriminability, spatial heterogeneity, and the need for multi-scale mapping of morphological priors. While convolutional neural networks address local textures via inductive biases, and Vision Transformers model global contexts through self-attention, neither paradigm simultaneously resolves these three challenges without incurring prohibitive computational overhead. Furthermore, clinical translation is frequently bottlenecked by human data scarcity. Here, we propose DualSeg, a dual-stage hybrid framework that unifies convolutional and attention capabilities through a synergistic local-to-global refinement strategy. The encoder employs Wave-Swin Blocks with dynamic propagation windows for hierarchical local feature extraction, followed by Vision Recurrent Weighted Key Value Blocks utilizing a novel Z-Shift operator for efficient, linear-complexity global context modeling. A lightweight decoder based on Non-negative Matrix Factorization subsequently fuses multi-scale features while suppressing background noise. On the murine KPIs and human HuBMAP datasets, DualSeg achieved mean DSCs of 92.98% and 89.79%, respectively. To evaluate crossspecies and cross-center generalizability under human data scarcity, we performed zero-shot inference on the KPMP dataset using models trained exclusively on murine data. DualSeg demonstrated superior generalization, validating its ability to leverage conserved mammalian morphological priors across staining domains. Code is available at https://github.com/unskye/DualSeg.

title: Self-Perceived Boundary Refinement via Uncertainty for Efficient Intrapartum Ultrasound Image Segmentation.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of the fetal head and pubic symphysis in intrapartum ultrasound is essential for automated angle of progression (AoP) measurement. With the increasing use of portable ultrasound devices, lightweight and real-time models are required. However, under such resource constraints, the limited representational capacity of lightweight models makes accurate boundary delineation particularly challenging. Existing methods based on explicit boundary supervision typically apply uniform supervisory signals across boundary regions, failing to account for spatial variations in boundary ambiguity and leading to suboptimal performance in challenging regions. To address this limitation, we propose FaburNet, a lightweight segmentation model that leverages predictive uncertainty as an adaptive signal for boundary modeling. Our key insight is that regions with ambiguous or missing boundaries naturally exhibit higher uncertainty than well-defined ones. Based on this, FaburNet exploits entropy-derived uncertainty as a self-perceived signal to guide boundary refinement, enabling the model to dynamically identify and focus on the most uncertain and error-prone regions. The resulting uncertainty map is further used to modulate feature refinement, directing the model to allocate greater attention to ambiguous boundary areas. This uncertainty-guided mechanism is seamlessly integrated into a lightweight architecture to enhance boundary details and preserve small structures. Experiments on three datasets show that FaburNet achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance among the evaluated lightweight methods with only 2.3M parameters and approximately 1 GFLOP. Moreover, it improves the accuracy of AoP measurement, highlighting its potential for real-world deployment.

title: Bias-Switchable Row-Column Array Imaging Using Fast Orthogonal Row-Column Electronic Scanning (FORCES) Compared With Conventional Row-Column Array Imaging.
abstract: Row-Column Arrays (RCAs) offer an attractive alternative to fully wired 2D-arrays for 3D-ultrasound, due to their greatly simplified wiring. However, conventional RCAs face challenges related to their long elements. These include an inability to image beyond the shadow of the aperture and an inability to focus in both transmit and receive for desired scan planes. To address these limitations, we recently developed bias-switchable RCAs, also known as Top Orthogonal to Bottom Electrode (TOBE) arrays. These arrays provide novel opportunities to read out from every element of the array and achieve high-quality images. While TOBE arrays and their associated imaging schemes have shown promise, they have not yet been directly compared experimentally to conventional RCA imaging techniques. This study aims to provide such a comparison, demonstrating superior B-scan and volumetric images from two electrostrictive relaxor TOBE arrays, using a method called Fast Orthogonal Row-Column Electronic scanning (FORCES), compared to conventional RCA imaging schemes, including Tilted Plane Wave (TPW) compounding and Virtual Line Source (VLS) imaging. The study quantifies resolution and Generalized Contrast to Noise Ratio (gCNR) in phantoms, and also demonstrates volumetric acquisitions in phantom and animal models.

title: Physics-Informed Implicit Neural Representations in Biomedical Tomography: Principles, Applications, and Reliability.
abstract: Biomedical tomography reconstructs spatially and temporally varying images or biophysical fields from indirect measurements governed by acquisition physics. Physics-informed implicit neural representations (INRs) parameterize these unknowns as coordinate-conditioned neural fields, optionally incorporating physical states, and estimate their parameters through measurement consistency. Despite growing adoption, the specific contributions of INRs are often conflated with those of forward modeling, continuous representation, and neural priors, obscuring when they offer substantive advantages. This review adopts a representation-physics-inference perspective to clarify the role of INRs relative to conventional voxel, basis, and other neural parameterizations. We examine how coordinate and state conditioning provide a direct interface to the forward model, while shared network parameters couple reconstruction updates across queried locations and states. Starting from scan-specific INR reconstruction, we identify three limitations: insufficient measurement information, modeling uncertainty, and the computational burden. Corresponding advances are organized into prior-enhanced reconstruction, joint estimation of target fields and physical variables, and scalable or amortized inference. Using representative examples from CT, MRI, ultrasound, photoacoustic imaging, PET, and optical tomography, we assess how these strategies affect reconstruction bias, identifiability, quantitative reliability, and computational efficiency. We distinguish essential, enabling, or merely incidental INR roles according to their coupling with acquisition physics. This perspective clarifies the opportunities and limitations of physics-informed INRs and identifies forward-model fidelity, solution identifiability, scalable inference, and independent quantitative and clinical validation as development priorities.

title: Beyond Morphology: Quantitative Bilateral Self-Referenced Frequency-Domain Diffuse Optical Spectroscopy Reveals Functional Abnormalities in Patellar Tendinopathy.
abstract: Objective Patellar tendinopathy (PT) involves functional and metabolic abnormalities that may precede structural degeneration, whereas MRI and ultrasonography primarily depict morphology. To bridge this gap, we aim to develop a quantitative optical method for detecting PT-related functional and hemodynamic abnormalities. Methods We developed an embedded multi-wavelength frequency-domain diffuse optical spectroscopy system integrating sinusoidal modulation, synchronized acquisition, real-time Goertzel demodulation, optical-property inversion, chromophore fitting, and standardized grid scanning over the patellar tendon region. To reduce inter-subject variability, a bilateral self-referenced strategy used the contralateral tendon as an endogenous reference. A composite optical biomarker, Tendon Hemodynamic Index (THI), was defined by integrating differential tissue oxygenation and blood-volume-related information. Results Phantom and in vivo measurements demonstrated robust quantitative performance. In a clinical cohort, THI was significantly elevated in PT patients and correlated with symptom severity and functional impairment across the full cohort, with Spearman correlations of 0.69 with the Numeric Rating Scale and -0.74 with the Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment-Patella score. In this exploratory cohort, THI distinguished PT from healthy controls with 91.8% accuracy, 95.8% sensitivity, 88.0% specificity, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.928. In imaging negative but symptom-positive cases, THI achieved 88.2% classification accuracy. In three exploratory follow-up cases, THI decreased toward the bilateral baseline as symptoms improved over 8 weeks. Conclusion The proposed method enables self-referenced quantification of PT-related functional abnormalities. Significance By revealing tendon hemodynamic abnormalities beyond structural imaging, this work supports early PT detection, objective severity assessment, and quantitative monitoring of disease recovery.

title: Surrogate Supervision for Robust and Generalizable Deformable Image Registration.
abstract: Objective Deep learning-based deformable image registration has achieved strong accuracy, but remains sensitive to variations in input image characteristics such as artifacts, anatomical content mismatch, or modality difference. We aim to develop a general training paradigm that improves the robustness and generalizability of registration networks. Methods We introduce surrogate supervision, which decouples the input domain from the supervision domain by applying estimated spatial transformations to surrogate images. This allows training on heterogeneous inputs while ensuring supervision is computed in domains where similarity is well defined. We evaluate the framework through three representative applications: artifact-robust brain MR registration, mask-agnostic lung CT registration, and multi-modal MR registration. Results Across tasks, surrogate supervision demonstrated strong resilience to input variations, including inhomogeneity field, inconsistent anatomical content, and modality differences, while generally maintaining competitive performance on well-curated in-domain data. Conclusions Surrogate supervision provides a principled framework for training robust and generalizable deep learning-based registration models without increasing complexity. Significance Surrogate supervision offers a practical pathway to more robust and generalizable medical image registration, enabling broader applicability in diverse biomedical imaging scenarios.

title: Synergizing SAM2 and U-Mamba as Mutual Teachers in a Dual-Branch Dynamic Knowledge Transfer Network for Orbital Segmentation.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of orbital structures in thyroid eye disease (TED) is critical for clinical staging and surgical planning. However, as an under-explored task, orbital multi-organ segmentation suffers from inherent data scarcity, resulting in substantial domain gaps when directly applying general-purpose segmentation models. These foundation models often lack sufficient exposure to orbital imaging data, producing anatomically implausible yet overconfident predictions. To address this challenge, we propose a Dual-Branch Dynamic Knowledge Transfer Network (DDKTN), which integrates the global semantic generalization capability of SAM2 with the fine-grained structural modeling strength of U-Mamba. Specifically, a Dynamic Feature Interaction (DFI) mechanism enables adaptively controlled inter-branch knowledge transfer, facilitating a progressive transition from SAM2-guided global semantics to U-Mamba-driven structural refinement. Moreover, a Bidirectional Consensus Confidence (BCC) regularization mechanism identifies consensus and discrepancy regions between the foundation and domain-specific branches, enforcing anatomy-aware consistency via mutual supervision. In addition, a Prompt Adaptation Module (PAM) leverages the anatomical sensitivity of the domain-specific branch to automatically generate structured prompts, thereby injecting reliable anatomical priors into SAM2. Experiments conducted on a private orbital CT dataset and a public coronal MRI benchmark demonstrate that DDKTN achieves superior performance, with average Dice scores of 93.68% and 94.65%, respectively. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component in improving generalization and anatomical fidelity. The implementation of our method is available at https://github.com/zltshadow/DDKTN.
